Title: Moral surgery: Negative revelations differentially alter retrospective evaluations of creators and creations
Authors: Sally MyungJin Shin, Paul Rozin, Gal Zauberman
Abstract: When individuals learn of a moral transgression committed by a creator they once admired, they face psychological tension: How do they reconcile their positive prior evaluations with this newly acquired negative information? While existing literature has primarily examined how such revelations alter current attitudes, we investigate how they trigger the differential reconstruction of past attitudes. Across five preregistered experiments, we reveal a robust pattern showing that individuals reconstruct their prior evaluations by separating the art from the artist. Specifically, although the revelation of a transgression prompts a significant downward revision in individuals' recalled evaluations of the creator, their recalled evaluations of the creation remain relatively resistant to the negative information. This differential memory reconstruction occurs for both experimentally induced and pre-existing positive evaluations, across multiple creative domains, and for varying levels of transgression severity. Furthermore, through targeted stress tests, we demonstrate that this observed phenomenon reflects a genuine psychological process rather than a methodological artifact. The effect is robust across incentive-compatible, multi-wave longitudinal, and separate measurement designs that rule out potential alternative explanations such as low cognitive effort, temporal proximity, and demand characteristics.

Title: When does perspective-taking predict coalition success? The interplay of propensity, accuracy, and social predictability
Authors: Anabela Cantiani, Ilja van Beest, Thorsten M. Erle
Abstract: Theories of coalition formation assume that coalition outcomes are determined by static features of the game (e.g., players' resources), because these features are thought to elicit universal allocation norms that allow players to anticipate each other's demands. Yet the same structural features can carry different social meanings depending on what players want, expect, and consider fair. Perspective-taking helps players navigate this social information, but its importance may depend on how predictable the social context is. We examined whether perspective-taking predicts coalition success more strongly when allocation norms are difficult to anticipate, than when norms are clear. We tested this hypothesis in two experiments using a real-time three-person coalition paradigm, in which we manipulated the predictability of allocation norms ( High-Predictable vs. Low-Predictable ). In Experiment 1 ( N = 851), perspective-taking predicted greater inclusion and higher payoffs only in the Low-Predictable condition. In Experiment 2 ( N = 1206, preregistered), we replicated the main effect of perspective-taking across conditions, but not its moderation by norm predictability. Exploratory analyses distinguishing the propensity to take perspective from the accuracy of doing so found that in the Low-Predictable condition propensity translated into coalition success only when paired with accurate inference of partners' norms; in the High-Predictable condition, propensity predicted success independently of accuracy. These findings showed that socio-cognitive processes play a relevant role in coalition formation, and that accuracy adds value beyond propensity only when allocation norms are less predictable.

Title: Perceived time in the presence of others: Further arguments for an attentional view of social facilitation
Authors: C. Belletier, P. Huguet, L. Ferrand, S. Droit-Volet
Abstract: Although the effects of the presence of others on behavior constitute one of the oldest topics studied in social psychology, the reason why these effects occur is still the subject of scientific debate. Three hypotheses are commonly cited: (1) the presence of others facilitates dominant responses by increasing arousal, (2) it captures attention, or (3) it increases the efforts of those being observed. Few studies have attempted to distinguish between these explanations, and those that have done so have used a specific paradigm: the Stroop task. In the present study, we proposed an alternative approach based on the use of the temporal bisection task. In three studies, the bisection results showed a temporal shortening effect in social presence (that of an experimenter) consistent with an attentional distraction-related effect. Our results also provided the first evidence that this effect may be stronger when the attentional conflict between the task and the presence is unimodal (e.g., visual task and visual presence) rather than cross-modal (e.g., auditive task and visual presence). They also suggested that the social presence effect might be similar to that produced by a mechanical distractor, although the social nature of the distractor increased the attention-related effect. We discuss how variations in the presence and behavior of the experimenter could contribute to the difficulty of replicating certain studies in experimental psychology, given that the social presence of the experimenter is generally assumed to be innocuous.

Title: Negotiations through the lens of situational affordances – A person-situation perspective on negotiating cooperation in social dilemmas
Authors: Dorothee Mischkowski, Jasper Zeno Siol, Isabel Thielmann
Abstract: We adopt a person–situation perspective on negotiating cooperation behavior in social dilemmas to examine when, and for whom, different forms of commitment (i.e., negotiation formats) increase cooperation. In a preregistered lab experiment ( N = 244), we assessed individual differences in prosociality and experimentally varied the negotiation format in a voluntary negotiation preceding an incentivized public goods game. We investigated the likelihood to take part in the negotiation as well as the final negotiation offer, expecting individual differences in unconditional vs. conditional concern for others (i.e., Social Value Orientation, Honesty-Humility vs. conditional cooperation and HEXACO Agreeableness) to be expressed as a function of the negotiation format. As expected, the likelihood to participate in a negotiation increased with conditional cooperation when negotiating common minimum (vs. individual) commitments. Unlike expected, final negotiation offers in individual (vs. common minimum) commitments were not more strongly associated with Agreeableness but exploratory analyses revealed a stronger association with Social Value Orientation. The results illustrate how situational affordances in negotiation situations help explain individual differences in negotiation behavior – and, ultimately, clarify which negotiation formats are most effective for whom.

Title: A signal detection analysis of source effects on misinformation susceptibility
Authors: Nyx L. Ng, Fabian M. Wurzinger, Bertram Gawronski
Abstract: Signal Detection Theory suggests that people may fall for misinformation because they are unable to discern true from false information (i.e., low truth sensitivity) or because they have a general tendency to accept information regardless of veracity (i.e., low acceptance threshold). While a large body of evidence suggests that characteristics of information sources can influence susceptibility to misinformation, it remains unclear how source characteristics affect misinformation susceptibility. Using a signal-detection approach, the current research investigated (1) whether source characteristics influence truth judgments of true and false information via truth sensitivity or acceptance thresholds; (2) potential differences between perceived reliability and perceived partisanship as distinct facets of sources; and (3) how the two facets interact with information content in shaping judgments of true and false information. Across seven preregistered experiments (N = 4,286), we found that (1) source characteristics affected susceptibility to misinformation via acceptance thresholds, not truth sensitivity per se; (2) effects of source characteristics were limited to conditions where comparisons of sources are salient; (3) source characteristics had no effect on partisan bias, in that acceptance thresholds were substantially lower for ideology-congruent than ideology-incongruent information regardless of the source; and (4) perceived reliability and perceived partisanship showed corresponding effects on acceptance thresholds regardless of information content, suggesting that both source characteristics might influence truth judgments via perceived source credibility. Together, the findings provide deeper insights into how source characteristics influence susceptibility to misinformation.

Title: Recovering from inauthenticity: Counterfactual thinking and the consequences of feeling inauthentic
Authors: Madelyn H. Church, Kianna M. Arthur, Kyle J. Dickey, Grace N. Rivera
Abstract: Counterfactual (i.e., “If only…”) thinking allows individuals to compare what has happened to what might have been, and may imbue both positive and negative events with meaning. Given authenticity's importance for well-being, we examined whether counterfactual thinking shapes affective and meaning-related responses to authentic and inauthentic experiences. Across four samples (N = 1359), participants recalled authentic and inauthentic events (order randomized), generated either counterfactual or factual details, and reported event-induced meaning in life and affect. In primary analyses on the combined samples, inauthenticity experiences elicited lower positive affect, greater negative affect, and lower meaning in life. Event type interacted with thought type, such that these affective and meaning in life differences by event were attenuated when participants thought counterfactually in the combined sample. Furthermore, affect significantly mediated the moderation of event and thought type on meaning in life, such that affect was a stronger mediator when participants thought factually than counterfactually. Findings were less consistent by individual sample, particularly regarding the interaction effects. This is discussed as an important limitation in conversation with robustness checks on the combined analyses. These findings provide preliminary evidence that counterfactual thinking may regulate emotional responses to authentic and inauthentic experiences, thereby weakening their association with meaning in life. However, effects on meaning were less robust and should be interpreted cautiously. Counterfactual thinking may therefore function as a double-edged sword when it comes to affect and authenticity, softening the negative impact of inauthentic reflection while dampening the positive impact of authentic reflection.

Title: Living beyond duty: People see meaning and happiness in supererogation
Authors: Ishita Singhal, Fan Yang
Abstract: In the timeless human quest for meaning and happiness, living a moral life has long been viewed as essential. But how do people determine which actions are most fulfilling? We find that when people evaluate the worth of morally good acts, it is not only what we do, but how society views our actions that matters. Five studies (N = 1800) across three cultures (U.S., China and India) examined if and how framing societal beliefs about actions as obligatory (fulfilling moral duty) versus supererogatory (exceeding moral duty) shaped people's judgments of meaning and happiness from moral actions. In Study 1, participants recommended greater behavioral prioritization and weekly time allocations to supererogatory (versus obligatory) actions, when giving advice intended to enhance meaning and happiness both for themselves and others. In Study 2, perceiving the same actions as more supererogatory was associated with greater meaning and happiness. Studies 3 (within-subjects) and 4 (between-subjects) experimentally demonstrated that framing identical moral actions as supererogatory rather than obligatory led to higher meaning and happiness judgments. These effects were mediated by inferring greater perceived choice and moral goodness from supererogation (Studies 3–5), and moderated by participants' own beliefs about the actions (Studies 5a and 5b). Similar mediation and moderation mechanisms were observed across the U.S., China, and India, except Indian participants associated even greater meaning with obligations. Together, these findings suggest that going beyond the call of moral duty is not just beneficial for society, but seen as rewarding in people's own lives too.

Title: Exposure to rising societal economic inequality reduces the misperception of racial economic equality
Authors: Sa-kiera T.J. Hudson, Julian M. Rucker, Bennett Callaghan, Michael W. Kraus, Leslie McCall, Jennifer A. Richeson
Abstract: People in the U.S. generally overestimate racial economic equality in contemporary society. A growing body of research suggests that the belief that the world is fair and just—i.e., belief in societal fairness—is a reliable predictor of the magnitude of these overestimates. The present work examined whether disrupting individuals' belief in the meritocratic opportunity structure in the U.S., via exposure to evidence of rising economic inequality, can subsequently reduce their tendency to overestimate contemporary racial economic equality. Across four studies ( N = 4512), including one high-powered, pre-registered replication with a nationally representative sample, we found that reminding people of rising societal economic inequality, compared with control information, led them to generate more accurate estimates of the current state of racial income and wealth equality (Studies 1–4). Further, restoring individuals' faith in U.S. meritocracy by informing them that social mobility in the country is still possible, despite rising economic inequality, reduced the effect of rising inequality information on racial wealth gap perceptions (Studies 3 and 4). We discuss the implications of our findings for both theory and social policy.

Title: Is honesty the best policy? Why people prefer false empathy over truthful unempathy
Authors: Zi Ye, Feiteng Long, Roujia Feng, Yi Zhang, Wilco W. van Dijk
Abstract: Literature of person perception suggests the primacy of morality over sociability in interactions. While theories of emotion highlight the importance of adhering to socially acceptable display rules, a contentious debate surrounds whether individuals prioritize moral or sociable communication of emotions. We investigated how people perceive and respond to others who falsely communicate empathic versus truthfully communicate unempathic emotions related to others' (mis)fortunes. Across five preregistered studies ( N = 1305), we examined participants' perceptions (sociability, morality, intent) and behavioral responses in a resource-allocation task using multiple paradigms (vignette, retrospective recall, and real-time interaction) and contexts (e.g., promotion, education, and lottery scenarios). Consistently, participants perceived targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions as lower on morality but higher on sociability and having more positive intent than those who truthfully communicated unempathic emotions. Moreover, despite the mixed findings regarding overall impressions, participants were consistently more willing to interact with and allocate resources to targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions. This preference was primarily driven by perceived sociability attributed to the targets. Together, these findings suggest that false empathic communication is favored over truthful unempathic communication, highlighting the relative primacy of sociability (and perceived intent) over morality in shaping responses to emotional communication in the context of others' (mis)fortunes.

Title: Smiling your way to happiness or misery? Experimental tests of competing perspectives [Registered Report - stage II]
Authors: Nicholas A. Coles, Annabel V. Dang, Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi
Abstract: Researchers and lay people alike have long been interested in whether people can make themselves feel happier if they simply fake a smile. Thus far, two largely disconnected research communities have provided seemingly competing answers to this question, with (a) emotion embodiment researchers observing positive causal links in experimental contexts, and (b) emotion labor researchers observing negative associations in real-world work contexts. In the present work, we conducted a pre-registered conceptual extension of the largest experimental demonstration of the positive effects of posed smiles on mood, focusing on three factors that may explain why such effects fail to generalize to real-world work contexts. More specifically, we tested whether posed smiles fail to improve mood (1) in negative contexts, (2) when performed repeatedly, and/or (3) when performed to avoid punishment. Ultimately, results did not support any one hypothesis. In negative contexts, participants reported higher levels of happiness after posing a single smile (vs. expressing themselves naturally). However, such effects were (a) diminished when posing smiles repeatedly and (b) virtually nil with the additional threat of punishment. Furthermore, in positive contexts, posing smiles repeatedly or under the threat of punishment led to lower self-reported happiness. Taken together, results suggest that posed smiles can be mood-boosting in some contexts and mood-dampening in others — a potential source of both happiness and misery.

Title: Reevaluating the empirical support for a lens-based account: dissecting comparative fit and reconstructive category guessing
Authors: Roland Imhoff, Verena Heidrich
Abstract: The lens-based account of intersectional stereotyping (Petsko et al., 2022) proposes that perceivers put on social “lenses” for categorizing their environment that exhibit comparative fit with observed behavior in a given situation. Support for this claim comes from studies using the Who-Said-What paradigm (Taylor et al., 1978), in which category membership was manipulated to covary with speakers' pro versus contra positions in a discussion along one of two crossed social dimensions. However, as noted by Klauer et al. (2014), this paradigm is vulnerable to a critical limitation: when category membership can be inferred from statement content, apparent categorization effects may reflect reconstructive category guessing rather than genuine category memory. Across three experiments ( N = 764), we tested whether comparative fit modulates social categorization beyond such reconstructive processes. We replicated strong comparative fit effects when category membership was inferable from discussion statements, yielding large effects comparable to those reported by Petsko et al. (2022). Crucially, when participants responded to discussion-unrelated statements that no longer allowed inference of category membership, these effects disappeared, indicating that prior findings were substantially inflated by reconstructive guessing. In a final experiment, we introduced an alternative source of situational fit by spatially aligning speakers with opposing discussion positions during encoding of discussion-unrelated statements. Under these conditions, a significant but markedly smaller comparative fit effect emerged. Our findings suggest that comparative fit can enhance social categorization along the fitting dimension beyond reconstructive guessing. However, this situational lens is rapidly “put off” once the fit is no longer present.

Title: When less is more: Unifinal framing promotes intention to use social media for social connection
Authors: David S. Lee, Daniel Kulesza
Abstract: People often wish to rekindle their dormant relationships yet struggle to act on their intentions. This intention-action gap is notable in an era of rising loneliness and surprising in a time marked by unprecedented technological tools for social connection. We propose that one reason for this gap lies in how people evaluate the appropriateness of the means for achieving their social connection goals. Drawing on goal systems theory, we examined whether framing social media platforms as serving a single social connection goal (unifinality) versus multiple goals (multifinality) shapes evaluations of the means and intentions to reconnect with dormant ties. Across three preregistered studies (N = 1095), unifinal framing increased perceived diagnosticity—the sense that a means is well suited to a focal goal—which in turn enhanced intentions to reconnect. Diagnosticity was empirically distinguishable from perceived instrumentality and more consistently accounted for the effect of framing on intentions to reconnect. These findings highlight goal structure as a key determinant of when people view digital platforms as appropriate tools for meaningful social connection and when they intend to use them for such purposes. We discuss broader implications for how individuals navigate their social goals in increasingly multifinal digital environments and for how technology companies must balance emphasizing multifunctionality with highlighting specific relational affordances.

Title: Everyday conceptualizations of patience
Authors: Samuel Murray, Devon Guzy, Áine Flynn
Abstract: People routinely use patience to interpret their behavior and the behavior of others, but the structure of these conceptualizations remains unclear. Across four studies (N = 1989), we mapped the cognitive prototype of patience and tested its robustness and consequences. Study 1 identified six definitive features falling under the categories of temporal tolerance, emotional composure, and self-governance. Study 2 found substantial relative convergence in multinational English-language definitions and in Spanish-language ratings and definitions from Mexico and Argentina. In Study 3, central features produced more false recognition and a more liberal response criterion. In Study 4, participants described a recent episode before seeing any mention of patience. Ratings of temporal tolerance, emotional composure, and self-governance jointly predicted subsequent patience judgments, and the combined prototype index predicted patience beyond practical success, overall handling, and context. Self-governance was more characteristic of self-control, whereas emotional composure was more characteristic of patience. Together, the studies identify a graded lay representation that recurs across different samples and organizes recognition and retrospective self-judgment. ResearchBox repository link: https://researchbox.org/6826 (CODE: FYLMZW).

Title: Bimodal emotion decoding: When faces and voices diverge
Authors: Hweemin Tan, Kerry Kawakami, Jinpeng Fu, Shuoan Li, Zhihe Pan, Xia Fang
Abstract: It is well established that people infer emotions from both faces and voices, yet how they integrate these cues when the two modalities convey conflicting emotions remains unclear. Evidence for facial dominance has typically come from studies contrasting facial and vocal expressions of anger and happiness, often using binary response formats that require observers to choose between face-consistent andvoice-consistent emotion labels. These findings, however, fail to inform us whether facial dominance reflects a general principle of bimodal emotion perception or whether these results are shaped by the specific emotion pairing and response format. Across six preregistered experiments (total N = 359), participants judged dynamic face–voice expressions spanning three incongruent pairings: anger–happiness, anger–sadness, and happiness–sadness. Experiments 1–3 used multidimensional ratings, and Experiments 4–6 used open-ended descriptions. The results revealed a pairing-dependent pattern: anger–happiness pairings showed robust facial dominance effects, anger–sadness pairings showed vocal dominance effects, and happiness–sadness pairings produced more heterogeneous impressions, including blended responses and third-category interpretations (i.e., anger or disgust for sad face–happy voice pairings). Together, these findings challenge a single-modality dominance view and suggest that bimodal emotion decoding depends on the specific emotions being integrated. To explain these pairing-dependent patterns, we propose and provide initial support for an emotion-similarity account, in which the relative influence of faces and voices depends on how distinguishable the competing emotions are within each modality.

Title: Evidence for ideological confirmation, or how to politicize color intensity perceptions
Authors: William P. Hart, Danielle E. Wahlers, Braden T. Hall
Abstract: Political groups may form based in genuine differences between people, but once formed, these groups and their associated identities can influence people's views and behavior. In line with social-constraint models, we tested whether liberals and conservatives would report arbitrary perceptual experiences because those experiences were situationally framed as signals of political identity. Participants completed a bogus diagnostic task in which perceiving colors as becoming either more or less intense ostensibly signaled possession of a liberal or conservative brain type. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants were told which intensity experience signaled brain possession prior to completing the task; findings showed that liberal and conservative participants provided reports of color intensity in ways that confirmed their ideological identity. In Experiment 3, participants were told which intensity experience signaled brain possession only after a trial on the task; still, participants reported experiencing color in identity-confirming ways. These effects occurred in college and online adult samples, among participants who indicated unbiased responding, and the effects could not be attributed to left- or right-wing authoritarianism; moreover, the effects were associated with self-judgments and evaluations of others. Political identities do not merely bias how people feel about value-laden political information; rather, they can influence people to adopt arbitrary social symbols that, once adopted, may create the perception of real divides.

Title: A preference for sameness and associated positive emotions in interindividual discrimination, even when based on chance
Authors: Xizhuo Zou, Fiona Kumfor, Evan Livesey, Leonie Schuppers, Eliane Deschrijver
Abstract: It was recently demonstrated that people allocate more money to another person when they both demonstrate the same outcome versus a different one, even when the outcome is based on chance. Different theoretical frameworks predict whether this effect reflects a preference for sameness, a derogation of difference, or both. Across three preregistered online experiments, we employed dot estimation (Exp. 1, n = 75), painting preference (Exp. 2, n = 75), and coin flip (Exp. 3, n = 84) versions of the sheer difference paradigm, while introducing a condition that lacked congruency information to distinguish these effects. Additionally, in the coin flip task, we explored retrospective emotional responses (using a self-report rating scale and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule-Short Form). We found that: (1) allocations in the sameness (congruent) condition were significantly higher than in the congruency-unknown and difference (incongruent) conditions (Exp. 1–3); and (2) participants reported more positive emotions in the congruent condition than in both the congruency-unknown and incongruent conditions (Exp. 3). Notably, the congruency effect in retrospective positive emotion ratings was also significantly correlated with the congruency effect in allocation measures. We discuss the use of congruency-unknown conditions in this study and in the wider literature to disentangle preference for sameness from derogation of difference. This study provides a clearer understanding of unequal allocation following interpersonal sameness versus difference, while also offering preliminary evidence for their relationship with emotions.

Title: Does online sharing drive attention to extreme viewpoints? [Registered Report Stage 1]
Authors: Jacob L. Orquin, Nathanael Larigaldie, Nick Simonsen, Sonja Perkovic
Abstract: Political polarization is often attributed to selective exposure, yet the mechanism by which online environments amplify extreme positions remains unclear. Attention is a precondition for downstream beliefs and behaviors, but existing theories of how it is allocated across political content have rarely been compared directly. In this Registered Report, we specify and test six theoretical accounts of attentional selection: selective exposure, the confrontation effect, decision difficulty, political acrophily, audience-response utility, and task-dependent attention, alongside a null account in which none of the theoretical predictors explain attention. Participants recruited online and stratified by political affiliation view 88 political posts, presented one at a time in a microblogging format, while webcam-based eye tracking measures visual attention. The ideological position of each post is defined as the median placement assigned by independent pretest raters. In the following condition, participants decide for each post whether they would follow the author; in the sharing condition, whether they would share the post on their own social media. After completing the main task, participants rate each post on personal agreement and perceived social-circle agreement. The theoretical accounts are represented by a preregistered set of mixed-effects models and compared using Bayes factors. The design tests whether selecting a source for oneself, compared with sharing a post with an audience, influences attention and, if so, which mechanism best describes it.

Title: Priming relationship pedestal beliefs in single people
Authors: Brittany E. Dennett, Burdett H. Kwon, Yuthika U. Girme
Abstract: Relationship pedestal beliefs (i.e., the belief that people need to be in a romantic relationship to be happy) has been linked to worse well-being. Yet, it is unclear if relationship pedestal beliefs can be primed. Across four pre-registered experimental studies (total N = 830), we tested whether exposure to a low vs. high relationship pedestal beliefs prime are associated with differences in the endorsement of relationship pedestal beliefs and well-being. Results from 3 of the 4 pre-registered studies suggest that participants in the high relationship pedestal beliefs condition (suggesting coupled people are happier than single people) reported higher endorsement of relationship pedestal beliefs compared to participants in the low relationship pedestal beliefs condition (suggesting single people are just as happy as coupled people) – although the lack of a control condition made it difficult to establish what direction the primes shifted beliefs. Exploratory analyses comparing experimentally primed vs. natural endorsement of relationship pedestal beliefs suggest that the priming effects may be limited to lowering (not increasing) relationship pedestal beliefs. Furthermore, the downstream effects of the primes were inconsistent across studies. Participants in the high relationship pedestal beliefs condition reported higher fears of being single (S2 and S4), relationship desire (S1 and S3) and negative mood (S2 and S4), and lower well-being (S1) compared those in the low relationship pedestal beliefs condition. Overall, we provide novel evidence that relationship pedestal beliefs may be malleable. Future research should establish directionality and consequences of exposing people to different narratives about single and coupled people.

Title: Glass half empty: How pessimism is seen as a moral failing
Authors: Eda Erensoy, Deborah A. Small
Abstract: Does expressing pessimism signal a lack of moral virtue? Across eight preregistered studies (N = 3952), forecasters who made pessimistic predictions about the state of the world in the future were consistently judged as morally inferior to forecasters who made optimistic predictions. This moral penalty persisted even when pessimism was evidently accurate (Study 3), and even pessimists themselves penalized pessimism (Study 4). These effects emerge because pessimism signals a lack of goodwill: Pessimists appeared less desirous of positive outcomes—a perception that undermined impressions of their morality. Supporting this mechanism, the same pattern emerged when pessimism was merely held in forecasters' private thoughts (Study 5) and disappeared when pessimists explicitly affirmed goodwill (Study 6). Examining more specific trait judgments, people judged pessimists as less generous, less sociable, and less likely to engage in moral behaviors—but no more honest and competent than they judged optimists (Studies 7a and 7b). These findings could have implications for which forecasters are trusted in society if societal pressures against pessimism influence communication about collective risks, crises, and global challenges.

Title: When racial violence becomes personal: how racial mega-threats transfer across racially stigmatized groups
Authors: Angelica Leigh, Tosen Nwadei, Marla L. White, Victor L. Marsh, Brian Lattimore
Abstract: Racial mega-threats–highly publicized acts of harassment or violence targeting members of racially stigmatized groups–are common in the United States. We propose that the harmful effects of these events can transfer to members of non targeted racially stigmatized groups through a personalization process. Specifically, outgroup racial mega-threats can heighten the salience of one's own group's vulnerability to racial harm (racial stigmatization salience), which in turn increases group realistic and symbolic threat. We further propose that this transfer is most likely to occur when perceivers believe that similar racial harm could plausibly affect their own racial group (perceived event likelihood). Across three studies, we find support for these predictions. In Study 1, mega-threat exposure (vs. control) increased racial stigmatization salience among Asian and Black, but not White, participants, which in turn predicted greater realistic and symbolic threat. Study 2 demonstrated that perceived event likelihood varied across racial groups and forms of racial harm. Event likelihood was higher when mega-threats reflected stereotypes shared with perceivers' own racial groups and was particularly high among Black participants for a mega-threat reflecting generalized racial animus. Using these differences to design stimuli that varied perceived likelihood of racial mega-threats, Study 3 found that Asian and Black participants exposed to higher-likelihood outgroup mega-threats (vs. control) experienced greater racial stigmatization salience, which in turn increased realistic and symbolic threat. These findings reveal that the psychological toll of racial mega-threats extends beyond the groups they directly target and identify when and why violence against one racial group can become personally threatening to members of various racial groups.

Title: Beyond ingroup vs. outgroup differentiation: Spontaneous racialized categorization reflects distinct groups
Authors: Nora Feline Becker, Juliane Degner
Abstract: Research using indirect measures has provided robust evidence that people spontaneously categorize others based on their racialized group membership. However, both theoretical and empirical work leaves unresolved whether such categorization reflects distinctions between specific racialized groups or a broader ingroup vs. outgroup differentiation. Research has predominantly relied on two-group designs, and the use of equal group sizes may have artificially influenced categorization effects. To address these limitations, we adapted the Who-Said-What paradigm (Taylor et al., 1978), a source-recognition task frequently used to investigate spontaneous categorization, to simultaneously include four racialized groups. Across two studies with White German participants, results indicate that spontaneous categorization indeed was based on distinct racialized groups. When group sizes approximated real-world distributions, within-group errors were higher for minority groups than for the White majority, suggesting that structural salience shapes the perception of racialized group membership. Together, these findings demonstrate the paradigm's utility for investigating social categorization in more complex and ecologically relevant social contexts and provide initial insights into the structure underlying spontaneous categorization.

Title: Registered Report Stage I: How intersecting identities shape perceptions of inequalities
Authors: Béatrice Sternberg, Amanda K. Sesko, Monica Biernat
Abstract: Research on perceptions of social inequality (e.g., in wealth, income, or access to health care) has typically focused on superordinate social categories (e.g., women in general compared to men, Black people in general compared to White people), while overlooking inequalities targeting intersectional group members (e.g., Black women). Bridging research on inequality perception and intersectional person perception, the proposed experiments investigate how intersecting identities shape inequality perceptions. We hypothesize that perceptions of economic inequality are anchored in prototypical subgroup members, thereby rendering multiply marginalized individuals less visible. In a Preliminary Experiment measuring income estimates, we found that perceptions of gender economic inequality for women aligned more closely with estimates for White women than for Black women, providing initial support for a prototypicality-based anchoring account of inequality perception. Two Registered Experiments will extend these results. Registered Experiment 1 tests the generalizability of this effect in the domain of racial economic inequality, examining whether estimates for Black people converge toward those for Black men rather than Black women, and directly examines the moderating role of perceived subgroup prototypicality. Registered Experiment 2 investigates if the same anchoring bias extends beyond inequality estimates to prescriptive responses by examining support for different types of equality-oriented policies. Unveiling prototypicality-based anchoring would challenge assumptions underlying superordinate-level inequality perception measures.

Title: A reanalysis of eye-tracking evidence for the diagnostic features account
Authors: Brandon Cohen, Debbie S. Ma, Tomás A. Palma, Eric M. Elias, Balbir Singh, Joshua Correll
Abstract: Research utilizing eye-tracking to investigate the cross-category recognition deficit (CRD) appears to suggest that specific features individuate different groups (e.g., that White faces are better differentiated by the eyes). In this paper, we present a reanalysis of the Burgund, et al. (2024) dataset, which includes three stimulus and three participant groups (White, Black, and Asian). By accounting for crossed random factors and the nonlinear relationship between looking time and recognition, we find that initial attention to facial features (eyes, nose, and mouth) tends to benefit recognition at low levels of attention. However, this relationship is characterized by negative curvature, indicating diminishing returns as attention increases, a pattern consistent with Correll et al. (2024). Furthermore, our results show that attention to a given feature benefits recognition, regardless of the race of the face or the perceiver. This pattern is inconsistent with the diagnostic-features account of the CRD (Hills & Lewis, 2006). We conclude that failing to account for nonlinearity and crossed random factors can distort the estimated relationship between attention and recognition, and that when these factors are modeled, the mapping from feature attention to recognition is the same regardless of perceiver or stimulus race. We discuss the implications of these findings for theoretical perspectives on the CRD.

Title: The effects of outgroup malleability and change motivation perceptions on collective action intentions
Authors: Smadar Cohen-Chen, Nathaniel Geiger
Abstract: Previous research suggests that perceiving high-power outgroups as malleable can empower low-power groups to collectively act by fostering hope, but may defuse intergroup anger, which also promotes collective action. We suggest that research on malleability perceptions, addressing the capacity for outgroup change, has overlooked perceptions about outgroups' motivation to change, which can lend insight to understanding the roles of hope and anger in promoting different types of collective action. Two experiments (N = 1823) tested the combined effect of outgroup malleability perceptions and change motivation perceptions in inducing different types of collective action intentions (normative, disruptive, and violent) through hope and anger. Study 1 used a between-subjects design in the context of interracial relations in the US. Study 2 examined liberals' attitudes toward healthcare executives following the murder of healthcare CEO Brian Thompson, using a 2 (malleable vs. stable outgroup) X 2 (motivated vs. unmotivated outgroup) design. Learning the powerful outgroup was unmotivated (vs. motivated) to change reduced hope and increased anger, which subsequently predicted collective action intentions; effects were stronger when the outgroup was perceived as malleable. Anger predicted disruptive and violent collective action intentions more strongly than hope did, whereas both emotions predicted normative intentions similarly. Correspondingly, in Study 2, learning that the outgroup was unmotivated to change increased disruptive and violent, but not normative, collective action intentions.

Title: Prototypes of Sexual Harassers
Authors: Sumayya Shaikh, Ignazio Ziano
Abstract: Across eight primary studies (seven preregistered; total N = 3009) and two supplementary studies with U.S. and French participants, we examined the content and consequences of sexual harasser prototypes. We found that laypeople believe sexual harassers possess specific psychological, social, and physical features (i.e., being tall, extroverted, unattractive, powerful, older, impolite; pilot study, Studies 1 and 2). Studies 3a through 5 showed that targets matching this prototype were more likely than counterprototypical targets to have ambiguous behavior classified as sexual harassment and to be seen as acting with sexual intent. Their alleged victims were also believed more and viewed as more uncomfortable and objectified, relative to those of a counterprototypical target. Study 3b indicated that these effects were concentrated on ambiguous rather than clearly non-harassing behavior. In Study 6, each prototype-consistent characteristic independently increased perceived likelihood of guilt, and ratings rose with the number of consistent characteristics. These findings show that an alleged perpetrator's resemblance to a sexual harasser prototype can shape judgments of ambiguous conduct, as well as its consequences.

Title: The role of intentions in punishment and compensatory decision-making
Authors: Anabela Cantiani, Alan Sanfey, Mirre Stallen
Abstract: This research aims to understand how people respond to harm by disentangling decision-making based on the intention to cause harm from decision-making based on the actual harm caused. Specifically, it examines how individuals process both intention and outcome information when evaluating harmful scenarios. The study investigates decisions to punish perpetrators or compensate victims in cases of intended harm, accidental harm, and unsuccessful attempts to harm. Additionally, it explores whether these retributive or compensatory choices are influenced by whether the participant is personally affected or merely witnessing harm to a third party.

Title: Feeling with family, grateful to strangers: Moral reactions to compassion and gratitude align with their social functions
Authors: Alexa Weiss, Pascal Burgmer
Abstract: Both compassion and gratitude are positive moral emotions that regulate relationships. However, the distinct effects of these prosocial, self-transcending emotions, particularly on third parties, remain largely unexplored. Drawing on research on social functions and on norms of emotions and relationship-specific moral cognition, two preregistered studies (N total = 640) examined social reactions (moral judgments and desire to affiliate) to compassionate versus grateful targets described in vignettes. We manipulated targets' social closeness toward emotion recipients (kin vs. strangers as sufferers/benefactors) and whether targets experienced the emotion toward a single individual or more strongly toward one than the other. As hypothesized, targets elicited more positive reactions when they experienced compassion with single suffering strangers than with suffering kin, in line with stronger norms to feel with family. For perceptions of grateful targets, relationships with single benefactors had less impact. More importantly, when pitting emotional reactions toward strangers and kin against each other, in line with our hypotheses, opposing patterns for compassion and gratitude emerged: Participants' reactions were more positive when targets experienced relatively stronger compassion toward kin than a stranger for identical predicaments. In contrast, targets who were relatively more grateful to a helpful stranger than helpful kin elicited more positive reactions. Both comparisons between grateful and compassionate targets within relational contexts and between relational contexts within emotions closely tracked theorized social functions of these emotions. Hence, moral reactions to similar prosocial, self-transcending emotions differentially depend on social contexts. By fulfilling emotion-specific norms, people may elicit favorable reactions from observers and potentially foster relationships.

Title: Willful ignorance in the context of antibiotic prescribing
Authors: Alina Schneider, Miroslav Sirota, Rian Gross, Lars Korn, Elisabeth D.C. Sievert, Cornelia Betsch, Robert Böhm
Abstract: Healthcare professionals tend to overprescribe antibiotics despite knowing the risks of antibiotic resistance. This tendency, amplified under diagnostic uncertainty and patient pressure, suggests that mechanisms beyond lack of risk awareness or knowledge sustain overprescription. One such mechanism may be willful ignorance – deliberately avoiding information about the consequences of one’s prescribing decisions. By allowing healthcare professionals to justify immediate antibiotic prescribing that prioritize short-term self-interests over long-term collective benefits, willful ignorance may contribute to persistent overprescribing. Despite its practical relevance, willful ignorance has not yet been investigated in the context of antibiotic prescribing. To test this empirically, we conducted two preregistered online experiments with healthcare professionals from the United States and the United Kingdom. Participants completed an adapted version of the Moral Wiggle Room Task, a behavioral decision-making paradigm designed to investigate willful ignorance. This task compares choices across a full information condition with diagnostic certainty, and a hidden information condition with diagnostic uncertainty that can be voluntarily reduced. In Experiment 1 ( N = 698), healthcare professionals were more likely to prescribe antibiotics immediately in the hidden vs. full information condition, supporting the presence of willful ignorance. In Experiment 2 ( N = 150), making the collective consequences of antibiotic prescribing for antibiotic resistance salient substantially reduced willful ignorance. These results highlight the role of willful ignorance in antibiotic prescribing and point to practical implications: promoting transparent environments and communicating the collective consequences of antibiotic use may help support more appropriate antibiotic prescribing decisions.

Title: When it is important to be more virtuous: Cultural tightness exacerbates moral superiority
Authors: Lipeng Yin, Zaixuan Zhang, Zhansheng Chen
Abstract: Moral superiority is a well-observed phenomenon associated with various negative consequences, making it essential to explore the antecedents of moral superiority. Employing a cultural perspective, we investigated the effect of cultural tightness on moral superiority, as well as its internal mechanism. Across five studies (N = 1040; three preregistered), we consistently revealed that higher cultural tightness increases moral superiority (Studies 1 to 5). Additionally, we found that individuals' desire for status accounts for this relationship (Studies 2 to 5). Moreover, we identified that the moral superiority induced by cultural tightness predicts individuals' tendency to treat others as means to an end (Studies 4 and 5). Collectively, our findings underscore the importance of cultural tightness in shaping moral superiority and introduce a motivational framework for understanding the relationship between these constructs. The broader implications and future research directions were discussed.

Title: Is comedy funnier when it is easier to process? The interplay of fluency and coherence in humor appreciation
Authors: Drew Gorenz, Norbert Schwarz
Abstract: Comedy needs to strike a balance between incongruity and coherence – it needs to present an incongruous surprise that nevertheless makes sense. Because fluent processing increases perceived coherence, variables that facilitate the fluent processing of comedic material may increase its funniness. Four experiments (total N = 999) with different comedic materials (visual memes, punchlines, and nicknames) and different fluency manipulations (contrast, rhyme, and alliteration) supported this prediction. In Experiment 1, internet memes were less funny when they were photoshopped to be harder to process visually. Additionally, people who self-reported more frequent exposure to memes in their daily life rated internet memes as funnier. In Experiment 2, participants chose rhyming or alliterating punchlines as funnier than non-rhyming or non-alliterating alternatives. In Experiments 3 and 4, aggressive and benign nicknames were rated funnier when they alliterated than when they did not. Serial mediation analyses supported a fluency-coherence account rather than a benign appraisal account. Fluency can facilitate the perception that an incongruity makes sense, increasing its humor. This pathway provides a promising framework for the conceptualization of numerous other variables known to predict increased humor appreciation, such as multimodal presentation, concreteness, identification as comedy, and laugh tracks, which may exert their influence by facilitating fluent processing and perceived coherence.

Title: How and why the omission bias affects victims' and third parties' responses to interpersonal transgressions
Authors: Justin M. Ludwig, Karina Schumann
Abstract: Prior research has identified an omission bias whereby third-party observers attribute greater intent, responsibility, and immorality to a transgressor for their harmful commissions than their harmful omissions. However, this research has not examined whether victims also show an omission bias in response to an interpersonal transgression committed against them, and whether these perceptions affect the apology-forgiveness process. We conducted four experiments ( N s = 376; 593; 595; 813) using complementary methods (hypothetical standardized offenses and real-life transgressions) to examine how and why commission and omission transgressions differentially affect victims' forgiveness, and whether apologies are differentially effective at eliciting forgiveness for these transgressions. We found that forgiveness was generally lower for commission (vs. omission) transgressions. Moreover, victims perceived commission (vs. omission) transgressions as higher in responsibility and intent, and these offense perceptions in turn predicted reduced forgiveness, both on their own and serially through judgments of immorality. However, apologizing (vs. not apologizing) predicted greater forgiveness for both types of offenses. In Study 4, we also tested whether victims' perceptions of commissions and omissions differed from third-party observers' perceptions. The effect of the commission (vs. omission) transgression on offense perceptions, moral judgments, and apology-forgiveness was similar across victim and third-party observer perspectives. These studies demonstrate how and why forgiveness might be less forthcoming for commissions than omissions, but provide evidence that apologies confer benefits for both types of offenses.

Title: Stimulus-category confounds reduce, but do not explain, different roles of intent across moral domains: Valid statistical inference helps explain ‘inconsistent’ findings
Authors: Joseph Sweetman, Ryan M. McManus
Abstract: The reduced role of intent when judging impure, vs. harmful, acts provides evidence that our moral mind/brain may be composed of distinct, domain-specific systems. However, a study that manipulated and statistically adjusted for the target (i.e., self vs. other) of the act reported a significant, but notably smaller, intent × domain effect. Recent studies that either manipulated or controlled for the context, severity, weirdness, and target of the act reported nonsignificant effects. We tested two competing hypotheses to explain these inconsistent findings: the intent × domain effect is a methodological artifact of the stimuli employed, or the effect is merely reduced in magnitude when controlling for potential stimulus-category confounds. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a close replication of one of the studies that reported null results. We found a small, significant intent × domain effect, supporting the reduced-magnitude hypothesis. We find that the “inconsistent” findings can be explained by the reduced magnitude of the effect when employing carefully controlled stimuli, and by whether researchers test support for the null hypothesis, conduct sample size simulations, and perform model checking and appropriate robustness checks when modeling ordinal (i.e., Likert) items as interval data. Indeed, the original study's null result becomes significant when an ordinal mixed model is fitted. Our findings are consistent with perspectives that view the moral mind/brain as constituted by multiple moral-cognitive modules. However, they are also consistent with a single moral-cognitive system with domain-dependent modulation. While carefully controlled experimental work and valid statistical inference help the replicability, robustness, and reproducibility of psychological science, delineating and decomposing the moral mind/brain will also require reforms to theory development.

Title: Underestimating sexism: Is gender categorization key?
Authors: Melanie C. Steffens, Franziska Ehrke, Karolina Hansen, Laura Loths, Jenny Dettmann
Abstract: In everyday life it can be controversial whether gender-based discrimination (i.e., sexism) has occurred or not. Claims of sexism are sometimes doubted, rejected, or cause backlash. The main aim of the present research was to investigate whether sexism is (relatively) underestimated. We experimentally tested whether instances of sexism are regarded as less discriminatory than the same instances involving racism, another prevalent form of discrimination (total N = 912). We developed a scenario measure to assess whether observers consider a wide range of everyday scenarios as more discriminatory in the context of sexism compared to racism as a reference category. Six experiments tested this with German and U.S. participants ( N 1 = 140; N 2 = 38; N 3 = 181; N 4 = 190; N 5 = 167; N 6 = 196). When the same scenarios described sexism, they were evaluated as less discriminatory than when they described racism against Black people (Exp. 1–4, mini meta-analysis, Exp. 6). This effect generalized to a different reference category (i.e., racism against Turkish people in Germany, Exp. 5). Delineating why sexism is regarded as less discriminatory than racism, we (a) found that perceiving sexism scenarios as less discriminatory than racism was consistently correlated with gender-related, not racism-related beliefs (specifically, endorsement of gender categorization and gender essentialism). A meta-analysis of each scenario (of Exp. 1–4) and Experiment 6 suggested that distinguishing “different” from “discriminatory” may be more difficult in the gender than race context. We discuss in how far acceptance of categorization may be key to ongoing discrimination.

Title: The subjectivity of objectivity: The effects of positionality statements on objectivity perceptions of psychological research
Authors: Sakaria Laisene Auelua-Toomey, Ellen C. Reinhart, Kengthsagn Louis
Abstract: The scientific ideal of researcher neutrality has historically been weaponized to delegitimize racially marginalized scholars, especially when studying the marginalization of their own communities. These scholars are often framed as biased, while White scholars are positioned as more objective. In response, critical scholars have challenged the myth of neutrality, arguing that all researchers bring positionalities that shape the scientific process. One tool used to counter the neutrality narrative is the positionality statement (i.e., disclosures of how researchers' positionalities shape their research). Across three large-scale studies (N = 4124), we examine how simple positionality statements (i.e., those that simply list researchers' social identities) can unintentionally maintain the very systems they aim to challenge. In Study 1, participants perceived anti-Sāmoan discrimination research as less objective when it was accompanied with a simple positionality statement from a Sāmoan researcher compared to one written by a White researcher. Study 2 shows readers' own racial identities shape these perceptions such that White participants were more likely than Black participants to perceive anti-Black discrimination research as less objective. Study 3 shows how the inclusion of elaborate positionality statements (i.e., those that explicitly connect researchers' positionalities to the research process) can mitigate some of the observed disparities in objectivity perceptions. These findings reveal how objectivity is racialized and how positionality statements might challenge or reinforce such biases. We discuss implications for the future use of positionality statements and offer recommendations for integrating them in ways that challenge dominant norms in psychological science.

Title: The perceived informational value of positive versus negative attitudes in impression formation
Authors: Tabea J. Zorn, Christian Unkelbach, André Mata, Hans Alves
Abstract: Positive and negative attitudes are not equivalent. Whereas people tend to like things for similar reasons, they often dislike them for different reasons. Building on the resulting greater diversity in the underlying causes of negative attitudes and the Evaluative Information Ecology model, we predict and show consequences of this asymmetry for impression formation in minimal-information contexts involving everyday attitude objects: People perceive others' positive attitudes (likes) as more informative than their negative attitudes (dislikes) and infer greater knowledge about a person from their likes. Across six preregistered studies (total N = 1100), participants reported greater perceived knowledge about targets based on their positive attitudes than negative ones. This asymmetry held across diverse domains (e.g., music, movies, sports) and could not be attributed to attitudes' frequency or participants' own attitudes. Instead, participants judged dislikes as more ambiguous, reflecting the greater diversity and disjunctive nature of negativity. This perceived ambiguity was statistically associated with the extent to which likes were seen as more revealing of the attitude holder's personality and broader dispositions. Finally, higher anticipated knowledge about people based on their likes was statistically associated with the relation between attitude valence and behavioral intentions, including information seeking and intention to meet the attitude holders.

Title: Do people think I'm late in life? An intersubjective approach to culture and the optimal timing of life
Authors: Lu Zang, Heejung S. Kim
Abstract: Individuals' personal beliefs, feelings, or expectations (subjective perceptions) often differ from what individuals believe most other people in their society think, feel, or expect (intersubjective perceptions). In this paper, we investigate cultural differences in people's intersubjective perceptions about the social clock—the socially prescribed age norms for engaging in important life events—and how intersubjective perceptions implicate subjective perception and prescriptive emotion norms. In three studies (all preregistered, total N = 675), participants from China and the U.S. were asked to provide the earliest and the latest ages they think a typical person in their culture would think appropriate for engaging in several life events. We found emerging evidence that intersubjective perceptions of the social clock were more rigid in China than in the U.S., and Chinese participants aligned their subjective and intersubjective perceptions of the social clock more closely than American participants did. Notably, filial piety beliefs are a likely explanation for cultural differences in the alignments. We further assessed anticipated negative self-conscious emotions (Study 1) and prescriptive emotion norms (Study 2) in response to deviations from the upper-bound of the intersubjective perceptions of the social clock. Further, Study 3 experimentally manipulated intersubjective perception of norms to test whether framing the intersubjective perceptions of the social clock as more flexible could mitigate anticipated emotional costs. The results inform the role of culture in associating individual perceptions and social expectations.

Title: Between law and conscience: Act legality shapes moral evaluation
Authors: Mane Kara-Yakoubian, Jonathan A. Fugelsang, Alexander C. Walker
Abstract: Can legality shape moral judgment? Across four experiments ( N = 1559), participants judged identical actions as more morally wrong when they were described as illegal rather than “not illegal.” This effect extended to judgments of moral character: individuals who performed illegal actions were evaluated more negatively than those who performed otherwise identical legal actions. The influence of legality was robust across several contexts, emerging even when agents violated the law unintentionally, when laws were imposed by a totalitarian government, and when actions were described as socially accepted by the majority of local residents. At the same time, legality exerted a stronger influence when it aligned with prevailing social norms and among participants who more strongly endorsed respect for authority as a moral good. We propose that people commonly use legality as a heuristic cue when evaluating the morality of actions and actors. Together, these findings suggest that legal frameworks not only reflect public opinion but also shape how people judge the morality of actions and those who perform them.

Title: We're near, they're far: On the association between one's gender in-group and psychological distance
Authors: Alys Ferragamo, Cheryl Jan Wakslak
Abstract: How does ingroup versus outgroup membership shape where people locate others across varied dimensions of psychological distance? Using gender as a window into this question, we recruited 2114 participants (265 college students and 1849 Prolific workers) across seven studies, examining whether individuals associate their gender ingroup with proximity across temporal, spatial, social distance, and hypotheticality dimensions. Adopting an initial exploratory approach and subsequent hypothesis testing, we expected participants' gender to moderate an association between gender category and proximity versus distance. Across four Implicit Association Tests (IATs) (Study 1A-1D), both men and women situated their gender ingroup (rather than gender outgroup) within a more proximal mental map – associating their gender with proximity in time, space, social dimensions, and sense of reality. Moreover, in line with prior work on asymmetrical gender associations, women exhibited stronger gender-distance associations than did men on three of the distance dimensions. Additional studies using explicit measures of gender-distance associations (Study 2 and Supplemental Study 1) and a scenario-based judgment context (Study 3) suggested that, particularly for women, these implicit findings extended to explicit judgments. We discuss implications of this work for understanding the impact of gender and of ingroup/outgroup membership more broadly.

Title: Registered Report Stage II: Defending or defying democracy? Investigating the relationship between conspiracy beliefs and support for democratic principles [registered report - stage II]
Authors: Tisa Bertlich, Felicitas Flade, Roland Imhoff
Abstract: Previous research on the relationship between conspiracy belief and democratic values is contradictory: there is evidence indicating that conspiracy believers are both less and more supportive of democratic ideas. We investigate this relationship using a fine-grained analysis of both plausible and implausible conspiracy beliefs and argue that even though conspiracy believers might perceive themselves as defenders of democracy, they are more likely to have antidemocratic attitudes. Furthermore, we propose two variables that could be responsible for the negative relationship between conspiracy belief and democratic principles. First, the reduced cognitive ability and motivation to process information associated with implausible conspiracy beliefs may undermine support for democracy. Second, a conspiracy worldview – shared by believers in both plausible and implausible conspiracy theories – may foster distrust towards those in power and, consequently, towards democracy as a system. Across three cross-sectional survey studies, we first establish that people who believe in implausible conspiracy theories are less supportive of democratic principles. Second, we find exploratory evidence for the idea that information processing could explain the relationship between conspiracy beliefs and support for democratic principles. However, we do not find robust evidence that the conspiracy worldview contributes to a lower support for democratic principles. To test the causal influence of both variables, we conducted an experiment in which we manipulated both participant's information-processing style and conspiracy worldview using fictitious vignettes. We found that an intuitive information-processing style contributed to a decreased support for democratic principles, while the relationship with conspiracy worldview depended on the political status quo.

Title: Prosocial by default: Defaults boost giving even under distraction and widespread non-responsiveness
Authors: Linh Vu, Margarita Leib, Jan Hausfeld, Shaul Shalvi
Abstract: Defaults are powerful: whereas wisely set defaults increase prosocial choices, poorly set defaults promote selfish decisions. In two preregistered studies (N Study 1 = 584, N Study 2 = 587), we test whether distracting environments, compared to distraction-free environments, make people rely more on selfish than prosocial defaults. Participants completed repeated binary dictator games in a 2 (selfish default vs. prosocial default) x 2 (distraction vs. no distraction) within-subjects design. Results from both studies and an internal meta-analysis provide no support for the hypothesis. Whereas participants accepted prosocial more than selfish defaults (in Study 1 and in an internal meta-analysis), the existence (vs. absence) of distraction did not affect default acceptance differentially for selfish versus prosocial defaults. Exploratory cluster analyses showed that around 75% of participants made choices based on their social preference, thereby showing little to no response to defaults. The remaining 25%, however, were responsive to defaults, resulting in an overall higher fraction of prosocial choices made when defaults are prosocial (vs. selfish). Overall, despite most participants being non-responsive, findings highlight the aggregate benefit of setting prosocial defaults, both in distracting and non-distracting environments.

Title: Revisiting Gino, Ayal, et al.’s (2009) contagion and differentiation in unethical behavior: A registered conceptual replication and extension
Authors: Jareef Martuza, Esra Aslan
Abstract: Individual behavior is often shaped by observing others' actions. The seminal Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) study found that individuals behave more dishonestly after witnessing blatant dishonesty by an ingroup member than by an outgroup member. However, because there was no group-irrelevant baseline condition, it remains unclear whether ingroup contagion, outgroup differentiation, or both drive the effect. Furthermore, using natural groups of university students leaves it unclear whether distinct properties of natural groups are necessary, or if mere categorization into arbitrary groups suffices. In this registered report, we tested Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) general hypothesis that exposure to ingroup dishonesty norms increases individual dishonest behavior more than exposure to outgroup dishonesty norms. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of their Experiment 1 with 3323 U.S. Americans using both minimal and natural groups. Participants were exposed to standardized information about others' dishonest behavior, where we systematically varied the group identities of dishonest others. Then, they completed an incentivized coin-flip task where participants could double their earnings by lying. Despite manipulation checks suggesting that participants processed norm information and strongly identified with natural groups, the pre-registered ingroup-outgroup hypotheses were not supported. Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence for null effects across comparisons (BF₀₁ = 3.15–14.71). The core ingroup-versus-outgroup prediction received particularly strong null evidence (BF₀₁ > 14). We conclude that exposure to ingroup versus outgroup dishonesty norms, delivered through descriptive statistics in online settings, might not differentially affect individual dishonest behavior, revealing a boundary condition of the original finding.

Title: Prosociality in times of war: Shared moral positions foster prosociality across national borders
Authors: Vanessa Clemens, Jasper Z. Siol, Lusine Grigoryan, Andreas Glöckner, Angela R. Dorrough
Abstract: In times of severe intergroup conflict, cross-national interactions are shaped by social categorization along national and moral dimensions. Yet, little is known about how these co-occurring identities jointly shape prosocial behavior. Across three studies (total N = 1178), we examined how shared nationality and moral position shape prosocial behavior during a real-world conflict (Studies 1 and 2) and a fictional intergroup conflict (Study 3). Moral positions reflected different moral values–judgments of war justification (harm/care) in Studies 1 and 3, and moralized responses to conflict behavior (loyalty/punishment) in Study 2. Using a crossed-categorization paradigm, participants played dictator games with interaction partners representing all four combinations of nationality and moral position: co-national with a shared moral position, co-national with a non-shared moral position, foreign national with a shared moral position, and foreign national with a non-shared moral position. Participants behaved more prosocially toward those sharing their moral position than toward those who did not, and toward co-nationals. These effects were additive rather than interactive. Across studies, the effect associated with shared moral position was larger than that associated with shared nationality, being approximately sixfold larger in the real-world context and nearly threefold larger in the fictional setting. Intergroup bias consistently increased with ingroup identification for morality-based, but not consistently for nationality-based identities. Differences in ingroup identification could not account for the stronger morality-based bias. Together, these findings suggest that, when multiple social categorizations are salient in cross-national contexts, shared moral positions represent an important basis for prosocial behavior alongside shared nationality.

Title: Sustaining your stance by speaking your mind: Expressing moral judgments increases certainty and prevents moral desensitization
Authors: Simone Mattavelli, Daniel A. Effron
Abstract: When news about another person's wrongdoing goes viral, people will hear about it repeatedly through social and traditional media outlets. Prior research suggests that this repeated exposure reduces how unethical people think the wrongdoing is – a moral repetition effect . The present research reveals that repetition no longer reduces moral condemnation when people express moral judgments upon each exposure, as they often do in the real world by commenting on news about wrongdoing. Drawing on attitudes research, we argue that repeatedly expressing moral judgments eliminates the moral repetition effect by increasing how certain people feel about their judgments. We found support in a meta-analysis ( k = 13 experiments, N = 6548 participants) and three pre-registered experiments ( N = 2637). The meta-analysis finds a smaller moral repetition effect for wrongdoings that tend to make people feel more (vs. less) certain about their moral judgments. Experiment 1 finds that people hold their moral judgments about a repeatedly encountered wrongdoing with more certainty when they actively express these judgments on each encounter. Experiments 2 and 3 show that prompting people to repeatedly express their moral judgments eliminates the moral repetition effect. These findings deepen our understanding of how and when repetition erodes moral condemnation and offer an actionable strategy to counteract repetition's effects. Encouraging people to express their views – rather than just to passively consume information – may help prevent moral desensitization to wrongdoing.

Title: Do people apply different norms to humans and large language models acting on their behalf? Evidence from norm elicitations in two canonical economic games
Authors: Paweł Niszczota, Elia Antoniou
Abstract: While delegating tasks to large language models (LLMs) can save people time, there is growing evidence that offloading tasks to such models produces social costs. We elicit appropriateness of behavior in two canonical economic games to study whether people have different norms for humans and LLMs acting on their behalf. More specifically, we study the social appropriateness of a spectrum of possible behaviors: when LLMs divide resources on our behalf (Dictator Game and Ultimatum Game) and when they evaluate the fairness of resource splits (Ultimatum Game). We use the Krupka-Weber norm elicitation task to detect possible shifts in social appropriateness ratings. Results of two pre-registered and incentivized experimental studies using representative samples from the UK and US (N = 2658) show three key findings. First, in the Dictator Game, the most socially appropriate allocation remains the equal split when the Dictator is a human or an LLM acting on behalf of a human, but self-serving allocations are judged less appropriate when implemented by an LLM. Second, in the Ultimatum Game, rejecting offers from an LLM Proposer is judged as more appropriate than rejecting identical offers from a human Proposer, with this difference concentrated among relatively generous offers. Lastly, rejection decisions implemented by an LLM Responder are judged no less appropriate than identical rejection decisions implemented by a human Responder. Post hoc, these patterns are consistent with the notion that people grant LLMs bounded agency in the investigated resource-allocation scenarios. Our findings have implications for the design of AI systems.

Title: Abstraction in service of connection: On people's recruitment of abstraction to facilitate interaction across difference
Authors: Alys Ferragamo, Yidan Yin, Cheryl Jan Wakslak
Abstract: People often interact with others who are different from them in some way. We examine people's beliefs about the usefulness of abstraction – focusing on the big picture rather than details – in facilitating these interactions, recruiting 1843 participants (688 undergraduate students and 1155 Prolific workers) to participate in six studies. We hypothesize and find that people tend to believe that abstraction is a helpful tool for forming connections across differences. Furthermore, people expect abstract thinkers to be more effective in situations that require working across differences compared to concrete thinkers; thus, people are more likely to assign abstract thinkers to these kinds of tasks. We also identify boundary conditions for these effects and discuss the theoretical and practical implications of people's beliefs about the functionality of abstraction in bridging differences.

Title: American liberals and conservatives have different cognitive styles, but (mostly) respond the same to party cues
Authors: Aymin Triki, Abigail L. Cassario, Mark J. Brandt
Abstract: How do people with different political ideologies process political information? The party cue effect is an effect where people are more likely to support a policy position if they learn their party also supports it, shifting their judgement in accordance with cues from their inparty and against their outparty. This effect has been at the center of the debate over the psychological differences between liberals and conservatives, with some scholars suggesting that differences in cognitive styles between liberals and conservatives (e.g., rigidity, cognitive reflection) should result in differences in party cue susceptibility. We advance this debate by measuring rigid cognitive styles and applying a stimuli sampling approach to party cues across four preregistered experiments (N's per study >1200). We found convincing evidence for ideological symmetries in party cues in quota matched samples of Americans (Studies 1 & 2). In Studies 3 and 4, across four measures of ideology and three self-report measures of cognitive rigidity, we found ideological differences in self-reported rigidity in line with previous research. In Study 3, a convenience sample, we found that conservatives were more likely to follow party cues. However, Study 4, using a quota matched sample, found no ideological differences in cue susceptibility, except with respect to right-wing authoritarianism. Exploratory analyses found that when one ideological group has greater prior awareness or stronger initial views on a topic, they show smaller cueing effects.
