We conclude that while liberals and conservatives differ in cognitive style, they largely share similar cognitive processes for interpreting and integrating political information.

Title: Can bad guys count as happy? The graded moralization of happiness across general and episodic levels
Authors: Jiangyong Li, Huaiyuan Qi, Jing Long, Yangmei Luo
Abstract: While philosophers and psychologists debate how morality shapes general happiness, episodic happiness remains neglected. Across three studies (N = 895), we provide evidence for a graded moralization account: moral character most strongly shapes general happiness (e.g., “leading a happy life”), moderately shapes social episodic happiness (e.g., “reuniting with friends”), and most weakly impacts nonsocial episodic happiness (e.g., “enjoying a meal alone”). Utilizing a vignette-based design with a neutral target baseline (Study 1), a preregistered familiar-target nomination (Study 2), and a preregistered replication (Study 3), we consistently found that immoral individuals were robustly denied general happiness, with ratings falling well below the scale midpoint. Moral constraints on episodic happiness were significantly weaker, diminishing from social to nonsocial episodes. Results further suggest the moralization of happiness may operate via distinct pathways. The denial of general happiness to immoral agents was consistent with intrapersonal inferences about their inner harmony and capacity for positive experience. Moreover, this moralization was qualified by just-world beliefs and malleable mindsets regarding morality or happiness. In contrast, moral constraints on episodic happiness were largely independent of perceiver beliefs and primarily sensitive to participants' own affective responses—reflecting a shift from abstract character-based inferences toward more stimulus-driven, situational evaluations. Nevertheless, a consistent similarity emerged across all levels: moralization was characterized primarily by selective downward denial for immoral individuals rather than upward enhancement for moral ones. These findings suggest a graded moralization of happiness, offering a nuanced model of how distinct dimensions of happiness intertwine with morality through divergent social-cognitive processes.

Title: Editorial Board
Corrigendum to “A trust inoculation to protect public support of governmentally mandated actions to mitigate climate change” [Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 115 (2024) 104656]
Authors: Tobia Spampatti, Tobias Brosch, Evelina Trutnevyte, Ulf J.J. Hahnel
Abstract: The authors regret to inform readers that an error occurred in where figures appeared in the originally published version of the article.Fig. 2: The image originally published as Fig. 2 was incorrect. It has now been replaced with the correct, original data intended for this location in the final article.Fig. 3: The content that was previously displayed in Fig. 2 has been moved to Fig. 3, which is its correct location according to the manuscript text and results. Title: Collective streaks motivate prosocial behavior
Authors: David E. Levari, Michael I. Norton
Abstract: We introduce a novel method for perpetuating prosocial behavior: highlighting collective streaks of behavior across individuals (e.g., “the last X people in a row have done it”). In 11 experiments (total N = 12,688), asking people to join a short ongoing streak of charitable donors was more effective than informing them of a high percentage of previous donors (e.g., “X% of people have done it”), because streaks increased feelings of personal impact on subsequent donors. Collective streaks can be effective even when their members are anonymous, and offer a way to encourage prosocial behaviors whether or not they are already popular: stating that 5% of people have donated is far from motivating, stating that 5 people in a row have donated induces further donation. Our findings illustrate how learning about the behavior of even a few peers can be a psychologically powerful motivator, particularly when they enable individuals to influence future others.

Title: People underestimate how receptive other people are to different political opinions
Authors: André Mata, Towe Nilsson, Arvid Erlandsson, Rosário Ferreira
Abstract: Four studies, with European samples, investigated receptiveness to opposing political views. In Studies 1a-1b, participants reported their own receptiveness and made inferences about the receptiveness of other people from either their most or least liked party. Results show that: a) people underestimate the receptiveness of other people; b) this underestimation is particularly strong for other people who support a party they dislike; c) they expect political conversation with supporters of their least liked party to be a negative experience, and have low intentions to engage in such conversation; and d) these negative expectations and intentions correlate with (mis)perceptions of receptiveness (i.e., the less receptive people expect others to be, the less predisposed they are to talk with them). In Studies 2–3, we provide further experimental support for the effect of perceived receptiveness on expectations and intentions to interact with political outgroup members, and we test an intervention to correct misperceptions of receptiveness. Implications are discussed concerning the relevance of perceptions of receptiveness in fostering dialogue and combating polarization.

Title: “Friend or foe?” the ironic effect of speaking the minority's language in intergroup conflicts: Palestinian reactions to Jewish-Israelis using Arabic
Authors: Slieman Halabi, Yechiel Klar, Murad Abu Elheja
Abstract: Speaking to others in their native language is often assumed to foster closeness and reduce conflict. Yet in settings of entrenched intergroup conflict, minority group members' reactions to being addressed in their mother tongue by the dominant group may be shaped less by interpersonal dynamics but more by histories of surveillance and cultural appropriation. Across two experiments, we examined how Palestinian citizens of Israel evaluated an Israeli-Jewish target who spoke in their native language, Arabic. In Study 1 ( N = 524), participants evaluated either an Israeli-Jewish or Palestinian target speaking Arabic or Hebrew; in Study 2 ( N = 781), a Scottish target was added to disentangle responses to non-native speakers from those tied to the conflict with the Jewish majority. Across both studies, when speaking Arabic, the Israeli-Jewish target, received lower personality evaluation, and elicited stronger negative emotions and heightened concerns about surveillance and cultural appropriation than when speaking Hebrew. Although some language effects also emerged for the Palestinian and Scottish targets, these effects were smaller and less consistent than those observed for the Israeli-Jewish target. These findings underscore the limits of intergroup interventions in contexts characterized by power asymmetry where the dominant group's use of a minority language may evoke distrust rather than fostering respect and inclusion.

Title: Giving women credit where credit is due: The role of amplifying, attributing, and appropriating others' ideas
Authors: Tara C. Dennehy, Holly R. Engstrom, Jo Hernanto, Toni Schmader
Abstract: Women are thought to receive less credit for their ideas in male-dominated group discussions. Five pre-registered experiments (total N = 2264) tested whether amplification (attributing an idea to the woman who originated it and asking her to elaborate) can ensure she receives appropriate credit. Experiment 1 provided preliminary evidence that appropriation of a woman's idea can lead people to misattribute that idea and credit that woman less for her contributions. Subsequent experiments found that amplification increased attribution accuracy and credit to women (Experiments 2–5), was similarly effective if the amplifier was a woman versus a man (Experiment 3) and can fully remedy the harms of appropriation (Experiments 4–5). Experiment 5 found that simply crediting a woman with the idea ( attribution ) was as effective as giving her the opportunity to elaborate on that idea. These findings suggest that amplification and attribution are viable allyship actions people can take to ensure their teammates receive credit where credit is due, with theoretical implications for literature on both source monitoring memory errors and signals of gender inclusion. [181 words].

Title: Hypocrisy either way: Judgments of moral actors who choose between conflicting commitments
Authors: Jonathan Z. Berman, Graham Overton, Daniel A. Effron
Abstract: People often make commitments to a specific behavior (e.g., eating vegetarian) in service of a higher-order value or goal (e.g., reducing carbon emissions). Yet behavioral commitments and the higher-order values they serve can sometimes point toward different actions (e.g., when choosing between a low-carbon meat dish or a high-carbon vegetarian dish). How are actors perceived when they choose to prioritize one type of commitment over the other? We find that in these situations, observers penalize them for hypocrisy regardless of which one they prioritize. Three main experiments (plus four supplemental studies; N = 3,340) document this hypocrisy-either-way effect across multiple scenarios and show that the act of choosing—rather than the act of committing to a behavior that could conflict with a value—is what observers find hypocritical. The effect emerges both between and within participants. The results illustrate an underappreciated risk of taking a moral stand: When actors adjudicate conflicts between behavioral commitments and higher-order values, either course of action can be judged hypocritical.

Title: Expectations of middle school children's academic performance in STEM and the Humanities: The effects of genetic and environmental frameworks
Authors: Lisa Luis, Mauro Bianchi, Rosandra Coladonato, Valentina Piccoli, Andrea Carnaghi
Abstract: This research investigated how genetic versus environmental explanatory frameworks influence adults' expectations about children's development of skills in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) and Humanities domains when both frameworks are cognitively available. Across four studies ( N = 1835), we employed a novel paradigm using gestational surrogacy scenarios to manipulate the salience of genetic (donors' educational background) and environmental (parents' educational background) frameworks. After reading the scenarios, participants evaluated the expected academic performance in middle school subjects related to STEM and Humanities for hypothetical children born via surrogacy. Participants' endorsement of essentialist beliefs (i.e., the extent to which they attribute abilities to predisposition) was also measured. Studies 1–3 employed within-subjects designs. Studies 1 and 2 tested the robustness of the paradigm using alternative versions of the material. Study 3 examined whether the effects were moderated by the gender of the child. Study 4 introduced a between-subjects design to test the relative influence of each framework. Across all studies, expectations about children's academic performance were shaped by both frameworks, but the environmental framework consistently exerted greater influence than the genetic in both STEM and Humanities domains and regardless of the gender of the child. Moreover, stronger endorsement of essentialist beliefs selectively enhanced the impact of the genetic framework, while leaving the influence of the environmental framework unchanged. The results are discussed in relation to the literature on genetic and essentialist beliefs about abilities relevant to STEM and the Humanities, with consideration of their practical implications.

Title: Testing the psychological distinctiveness of proscriptive and prescriptive moral norms: A replication and extension of
Authors: Andrew Miles, Yagana Samim, Salwa Khan
Abstract: The division between the prescriptive and proscriptive—between “shoulds” and “should nots”—is fundamental to morality. Janoff-Bulman and colleagues (2009) argued that the two are psychologically distinct, with proscriptive moral norms being more concrete and obligatory, and their violation seen as more negative, than prescriptive norms. However, the evidence supporting claims of distinctiveness is relatively sparse and occasionally mixed, leaving the implications of the proscriptive/prescriptive distinction for behavior, emotions, and other outcomes unclear. In three studies, we test for differences between these two types of morality using exact and conceptual replications of prior work, and we examine the generalizability of the differences we find across demographic groups who differ in their moral worldviews. Our results indicate that differences between proscriptive and prescriptive moral norms run mainly along the lines of negativity and—to a lesser degree—concreteness. The pattern of results generalizes across demographic groups, hinting at wide applicability. These findings support the psychological distinctiveness of proscriptive and prescriptive morality.

Title: Fairness matters: The impact of leaders' emotional expressions on subordinates' behavior
Authors: Adili Abudukadier, Zhikun Zhou, Zhijun Cheng, Xudong Wang, Yangmei Luo, Xuhai Chen
Abstract: Leaders' emotional expressions potently influence employee behavior, yet the moderating role of fairness in this process remains under-explored. The present research investigates how and why the perceived fairness of a leader's emotions shapes follower outcomes at both the individual and dyadic levels. Across a scenario-based experiment (Study 1) and a controlled laboratory study with an interactive task (Study 2), we consistently found that a leader's expression of happiness (vs. neutrality) elicited more positive emotions, greater effort, and enhanced cooperation in followers, but these effects were modulated by the fairness of leader's expression. Consistent with the Emotions as Social Information (EASI) model, a structural equation model revealed that behavioral effect was mediated by followers' affective experiences and cognitive inferences, with fairness moderating these mediating pathways. Furthermore, Study 2 incorporated electroencephalography (EEG) and hyperscanning, identifying event-related potentials (N1, LPP, SPW) and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) as neural markers of this moderated process. By integrating organizational psychology and cognitive neuroscience, these findings specify fairness as a critical boundary condition for the social effects of emotions, advancing the EASI model by elucidating the neurocognitive mechanisms through which fair emotional displays foster team coordination.

Title: Does attending to the nose vs. eyes reduce the cross-race recognition deficit? A systematic test
Authors: Tomás A. Palma, Francisco Cruz, Joana Quarenta, Joshua Correll, Marco Carvalho, Marta Barros, Debbie Ma
Abstract: People typically demonstrate poorer recognition for faces from racial outgroups compared to ingroups, a phenomenon known as the cross-race recognition deficit (CRD). In the present research, we tested one influential account of this effect: the diagnostic-features model. This model proposes that, through experience, the perceptual system becomes tuned to race-specific diagnostic features (e.g., eyes for White faces, nose for Black faces), and that directing attention to these features can reduce the CRD. We systematically tested this prediction across five studies ( N = 736) using face stimuli drawn from six databases. In Studies 1 to 4, White (Portuguese) participants completed old/new recognition tasks with both White and Black faces, using either fixation crosses (Studies 1, 2, 4) or explicit word cues (Study 3) to direct attention to the eyes or nose. Study 5 extended the design in three ways: it recruited UK-born participants, included both White and Black perceivers, and used both male and female faces, thereby more closely aligning the design with the original studies while adding methodological improvements. Across all five studies, we consistently observed the CRD, but found no credible evidence that directing attention to putatively diagnostic features modulated the CRD, with Bayes factors providing strong evidence against this effect. The absence of a fixation effect held equally for White and Black perceivers and for male and female faces. Together, these findings are difficult to reconcile with the diagnostic-features account as originally formulated, while remaining compatible with the more limited possibility that face individuation relies on more similar information across racial groups than the account assumes.

Title: Selective ignorance? The role of the information target in allocation decisions
Authors: Hagit Sabato, Ilana Ritov
Abstract: Previous research has demonstrated the tendency to avoid information about consequences of one's behavior, as a way of acting selfishly while still preserving a positive self-image. In the present research we propose that altruistic motivation may also be linked to information avoidance, particularly when the missing information pertains to the decision-maker themselves rather than to a passive recipient. In two preregistered studies ( N = 500), using between- and within-subjects designs, we examined participants' allocation decisions as a function of their decision to avoid information about payoffs, while manipulating whether the missing information referred to oneself or the other. Results revealed a consistent pattern across studies: when the missing information referred to the other, avoiding it was significantly associated with less prosocial choices. Conversely, when the missing information referred to oneself (i.e., the participant's own payoff), avoidance was significantly associated with more prosocial choices. This finding highlights the role of the social and moral contexts in which ignorance occurs, suggesting a more nuanced understanding of when ignorance serves self-interest and when it may instead support prosocial motivation.

Title: Is it my fault? How attributing exclusion to norm violations triggers self-directed emotions
Authors: Larissa C. Damp, Selma C. Rudert
Abstract: Being excluded hurts, but does it always hurt in the same way? Previous research has mostly treated social exclusion as uniformly painful, yet in everyday life, exclusion typically comes with context and reasons. We propose that beyond the general distress of being excluded, self-directed emotions such as guilt, shame, and self-directed anger emerge when targets can identify why they were excluded, recognize the cause as something they could have acted on differently, and construe the exclusion as deserved. Across four preregistered studies ( N = 1757), we tested this proposition using norm violations as a prototypical self-implicating attribution and paradigms in which participants experienced exclusion in real time rather than recalling or imagining it. Across studies, norm-based exclusion consistently elevated self-directed emotions, with perceived deservingness showing the most consistent association with these responses. Critically, Study 4 showed that an alternative attribution (Gender-based exclusion) did not elevate self-directed emotions relative to a baseline condition without explanation, pointing to controllable, self-implicating attributions and the resulting sense of deservingness as the features most closely associated with self-directed responses. Together, these findings suggest that exclusion's emotional impact depends on the attributional meaning targets assign to it.

Title: Persuasion via intermediaries: The pull of extremity
Authors: Derek D. Rucker, Mark Dyer, Jesse D'Agostino, Zakary L. Tormala
Abstract: Persuasion is a powerful device for shaping people's attitudes and actions. Recent work has begun to examine who persuaders target with their persuasive efforts. The current work explores how persuaders think about intermediaries—individuals who can advocate to a target on the persuader's behalf. Specifically, this work studies people's preferences to seek breadth of support—prioritizing the number of intermediaries with favorable attitudes—versus depth of support—prioritizing extreme attitudes among intermediaries. Although advantages exist to both approaches, six initial experiments with varied paradigms document a preference for depth: persuaders favor obtaining support from fewer intermediaries with more extreme attitudes compared to more intermediaries with less extreme attitudes. To explain these results, two additional experiments demonstrate that people believe intermediaries with more extreme attitudes are more likely to invest the necessary effort and intensity to advocate for the persuader's position and therefore are perceived as more likely to persuade the target. Building on this mechanism, two final experiments demonstrate that persuaders' preference for depth versus breadth is moderated by whether people believe effort and intensity are required by intermediaries. Implications for understanding how people think about using intermediaries, as well as targeting in persuasion more generally, are discussed.

Title: Cognitive conflict in willful ignorance: A mouse-tracking study
Authors: Fiona tho Pesch, Anna Baumert
Abstract: People sometimes ignore information that could inform their decisions. In prosocial contexts, willful ignorance is thought to help individuals avoid cognitive conflict when acting selfishly. To test this, we tracked participants' mouse trajectories while they made binary, incentivized decisions about allocating money between themselves and a charity ( N = 210). In an initial phase, participants could ignore the impact of their decision on the charity. In a second phase, 18 decisions were made without this option, with 12 involving a self-other tradeoff. Our results showed that participants who engaged in willful ignorance displayed mouse trajectories that were more strongly curved towards the non-chosen option, indicating greater cognitive conflict. Additionally, selfish choices were associated with mouse trajectories indicating greater cognitive conflict, moderated by individual differences: dispositionally prosocial individuals displayed less conflict when choosing prosocially, whereas dispositionally selfish individuals displayed conflict regardless of choice. These findings suggest that willful ignorance may serve as a strategy to manage decision-related conflict, particularly for dispositionally selfish individuals.

Title: Seeing oneself in the feed: Racialized targeting in food marketing and its impact on adolescents' visual interest and unhealthy food preferences
Authors: Emily Balcetis, Jordan Daley, Eunha Choi, Omni Cassidy, Marie A. Bragg
Abstract: What psychological mechanisms make the marketing of unhealthy foods to racial and ethnic minority adolescents persuasive? We proposed that social media promoters who share adolescents' racial or ethnic identity are more interesting to look at than incongruent promoters especially to minority adolescents, and that social modeling of these visually interesting promoters increases susceptibility to choosing unhealthy foods. In two experiments (total n = 1408), we tested the impact of visual interest in mock Instagram posts that featured promoters who did or did not share the same race/ethnicity as participants and who were depicted as endorsing unhealthy food or non-food products on adolescents' food choices. In Study 1, Black, but not non-Hispanic White, adolescents reported that racially congruent promoters were more visually interesting than incongruent promoters. In Study 2, minority adolescents who identified as Black, Hispanic, or East Asian reported that congruent promoters were more visually interesting than incongruent promoters. Non-Hispanic White adolescents did not report more interest in congruent, White promoters than incongruent promoters. In both studies, increased visual interest predicted an increase in unhealthy snack selections, but only when the posts endorsed unhealthy foods. We also found that visual interest predicted higher engagement with posts, reflected in stronger likelihood of “liking,” commenting, or sharing the post. These findings reveal visual interest as a key attentional mechanism linking identity congruence to persuasion, advancing theories of motivated attention and informing strategies to counteract the influence of racially targeted food marketing.

Title: Diversity, equity, and inclusion regression: Perceptions of organizations that fail to persevere in their stated commitments
Authors: Kim E. Chaney, Izilda Pereira-Jorge
Abstract: U.S. organizations have increasingly abandoned their commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). The present research examines whether assessments of an organization's motivation to be non-prejudiced and anticipated identity safety at an organization are impacted by the organization's perseverance in their DEI commitment. Across four experiments with Black Americans (N = 1375), organizations that had diversity statements two years ago and have either removed or diluted this statement in the present were perceived as less genuinely committed to be non-prejudiced, less tenacious in their DEI commitments, and signaled less anticipated belonging for Black Americans compared to an organization that has persisted in its commitment. These effects emerged even when anti-DEI state legislation (Study 2) and norms of DEI regression across organizations (Study 3) were made salient. These findings demonstrate that perseverance of organizational identity safety cues is critical in shaping attributions of motivations and identity safety.

Title: People feel but don't tell: Dispositional honesty and emotional responses to others' (mis)fortunes
Authors: Zi Ye, Feiteng Long, Roujia Feng, Wilco van Dijk, Ranran Li
Abstract: People experience a range of emotions in response to others' fortunes and misfortunes, from empathic emotions (e.g., happy-for-ness, sympathy) to unempathic emotions (e.g., schadenfreude, glückschmerz). A central question is whether such emotions are communicated as they are genuinely experienced or strategically adjusted to meet social and interpersonal norms. Across three preregistered studies (N = 701), we examined whether Honesty-Humility – a core dimension of moral personality in the HEXACO model – shapes both the experience and communication of these emotions. Participants reported their experienced and communicated emotions using hypothetical scenarios (Study 1), retrospective self-reports (Study 2), and real-time interpersonal interaction (Study 3). Results from Studies 1 and 2 showed that lower Honesty-Humility was associated with a greater tendency to selectively downplay unempathic emotions in communication, whereas exaggeration of empathic emotions was not observed. Honesty-Humility was also negatively related to the experience of unempathic emotions, with no consistent association for empathic emotions. Although dispositional effects were attenuated in real-time interaction, an internal meta-analysis supported their overall robustness. By distinguishing emotional experience from emotional expression, this research advances understanding of emotional communication as a socially strategic yet morally constrained process, and integrates personality perspectives with the Emotion as Social Information (EASI) framework, the tension between honesty and prosociality, and loss aversion.

Title: Selective traits and general rewards: Differentiating learning effects on social impression and choice
Authors: Kira Harris, Andrew Luttrell, Peter Mende-Siedlecki, Leor M. Hackel
Abstract: People learn about their social world by inferring traits others possess (e.g., “generous”), allowing them to flexibly predict others' behavior in new settings. Yet, people also experience rewarding outcomes in social interactions (e.g., getting a gift). Rewards feel good and may cast a positive glow on others. We tested whether people apply these two types of learning differently to new circumstances. Specifically, we hypothesized that rewards lead to a more general positivity toward others, across judgments and choices, than trait inferences, which exert a more selective influence. In four experiments (N = 52, N = 100, N = 91, N = 182), online participants recruited from the university participant pool and Prolific learned about others in a sharing game. These individuals independently varied in reward value to the participant (the absolute amount of money they provided) and their generosity (the proportion of available money they shared). Participants made decisions across games, hypothetical scenarios, and trait ratings that varied in relevance to the sharing game. Participants used trait feedback more selectively than reward feedback: they preferred generous partners more in settings more relevant to generosity, but they preferred previously rewarding partners to a similar degree across scenarios and trait ratings. These results suggest a small, more consistent influence of rewarding outcomes on person representations, compared to trait learning's more selective influence. Beyond reinforcing behaviors, rewards lead people to ascribe positive attributes to and feel drawn toward rewarding individuals more consistently than traits, which convey specific meaning that people apply based on relevance.

Title: Replication and extension of Carlson and Zaki (2018): Do lay theories of altruism apply equally to all actors?
Authors: Ashley Harrell, Margaret L. Traeger
Abstract: Observers rely on perceived motives when evaluating prosocial behavior. Carlson and Zaki (2018) demonstrate that helping typically earns actors altruistic “credit” compared to neutral activities—but helping for self-interested reasons produces penalties, leading actors to be judged as less altruistic than those who do not help at all. Here we ask whether these patterns operate similarly across actors who differ by race (in our study, Black or White) and gender (male or female)—social categories that carry well-documented expectations and stereotypes regarding communality, trustworthiness, and moral character. Across two high-powered studies using the vignettes and key measures from Carlson and Zaki (2018), 3185 participants evaluated actors who engaged in neutral acts or helpful acts with or without self-interested motives for helping. We replicate Carlson and Zaki's key findings: actors who help are perceived as more altruistic than those who engage in neutral acts, while those who help with self-interested motives are seen as less altruistic than those who do not help at all. Extending this framework, we find no substantively meaningful differences in either credit for helping or penalties for self-interested helping by the actor's race, gender, or their interaction. Our findings suggest that, despite gendered and racialized stereotypes about communality and morality, observers rely primarily on inferred motives—rather than social category membership—when translating helping behavior into moral reputation.

Title: Editorial Board
Smiling your way to happiness or misery? Experimental tests of competing perspectives
Authors: Nicholas A. Coles, Annabel Dang, Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi

Title: Incentivization very weakly improves theory of mind: A multi-sample investigation and meta-analysis
Authors: Tomer Paz-Fitussy, Eldad Yechiam
Abstract: Previous studies showed inconsistent results with respect to the impact of financial incentivization on Theory of Mind (ToM) indices, with some theoretical frameworks arguing for a positive influence of effortful attention caused by incentives, and others for a negative influence. In five samples we examined both the effect of incentivization as well as potential moderators, including the type of ToM (emotional vs. cognitive), gender, and task difficulty. Additionally, three of the samples were drawn from a general population of online workers and two included only individuals who stated they had ADHD. The results showed that across the five samples (n = 1915) there was a very small effect of incentivization on identifying emotions in faces and identifying faux pas (Cohen's d = 0.12, 0.07, respectively), that was not significant across tasks. The effect was somewhat higher and was significant for women (d = 0.18 across tasks) but not for men. In a meta-analysis of the literature on identifying emotions in faces, the very small effect size of incentivization was replicated (d = 0.13). These findings suggest that certain unique aspects of ToM tasks “crowd out” the impact of incentives, resulting in smaller positive effect sizes than those typically observed in other cognitive tasks.

Title: Beliefs versus reality: People overestimate the actual dishonesty of others
Authors: Jareef Martuza, Helge Thorbjørnsen, Hallgeir Sjåstad
Abstract: Do people believe that others are similarly, more, or less dishonest than they truly are? The accuracy of dishonesty beliefs is not only important for psychological knowledge, but also has implications for organizations and policymaking. In this paper, Study 1 presents a research program on moral decision-making comprising 31 different effects from 11 experiments, where participants could anonymously lie for personal gain. Crucially, participants were also asked to estimate what percentage of other people would lie in the same situation. An internal meta-analysis summarizing all belief-behavior comparisons revealed that people substantially overestimate others' dishonest behavior ( g = 0.61; k = 31; N = 8126), by 13.6 percentage points on average. This effect holds across study contexts and participants' own behavior, and 63.5% of participants overestimated dishonesty by 5 percentage points or more (only 25.4% underestimated it). We then examined potential consequences of biased dishonesty beliefs in three pre-registered follow-up studies. Study 2 ( N = 981) found that providing correct information about actual honesty levels enhanced general prosocial expectations (e.g., trustworthiness, fairness). Study 3 ( N = 285) revealed that professional managers have pessimistic beliefs also about people's real-world dishonesty (e.g., insurance fraud, workplace theft), and moral pessimism predicted greater support for freedom-restrictive countermeasures to reduce dishonesty (e.g., surveillance). Study 4 ( N = 741) demonstrated that providing managers with correct information about actual honesty levels causally reduced their support for freedom-restrictive countermeasures. In conclusion, the pessimistic bias in dishonesty beliefs about others is robust, and it shapes prosocial expectations and policy preferences.

Title: Just a means to an end? Individuals support direct democracy instrumentally, irrespective of conspiracy mentality
Authors: Tisa Bertlich, Fiona Kazarovytska, Roland Imhoff
Abstract: Conspiracy beliefs are considered a challenge to current democracies. One reason for this is that conspiracy believers tend to be less satisfied with the political status quo and more supportive of alternative types of governing, such as direct democracies. To gain a deeper understanding of this relationship, we investigated whether the relationship between conspiracy mentality, the general tendency to see conspiracies happening in society, and support for direct democracy is fueled by intrinsic values attributed to direct democratic decision-making or by the perceived personal benefit gained from it. In four pre-registered experimental studies (overall N = 1319), we informed participants whether their opinion on specific policies was shared by the majority or the minority of citizens. Subsequently, we asked them for their support for direct-democratic decision-making on this topic. The results indicate that, in general, people are more supportive of direct democratic decision-making when they think the majority shares their opinion, and people with a stronger conspiracy mentality tend to be more supportive of direct democracy. However, we found no evidence that conspiracy mentality moderates the effect of holding a position shared by the majority (vs minority) on support for direct democracy. An internal meta-analysis of the four experiments also found no evidence of such a moderation effect. Taken together, albeit previous research indicates that conspiracy believers are especially self-centered, our findings indicate that they are just as much influenced by majority and minority perceptions of public opinions as other people.

Title: Managing threatened identities across everyday situations
Authors: N. Derek Brown, Drew S. Jacoby-Senghor, Allyson P. Mackey, Michael L. Slepian
Abstract: Identity threats occur across diverse identities and situations, yet little is known about how responses to these threats relate to subsequent psychological costs across diverse identities, people, and situations. Across six studies capturing 22,000+ instances of identity threat experienced by 1648 participants, we identify two prevalent identity distancing strategies: downplaying a threatened identity and emphasizing similarity to others. Correlational evidence (Studies 1–3) illustrates that greater downplaying of identities most strongly predicted feeling inauthentic, whereas greater downplaying and emphasizing similarly predicted disidentifying from the threatened identity. Identity distancing predicted felt inauthenticity regardless of social climate or concealability, whereas disidentification depended on these contextual factors, underscoring when identity distancing may be adaptive. Finally, both strategies indirectly predicted greater psychological stress and worse self-reported physical health through inauthenticity and disidentification. Extending beyond correlational findings, a longitudinal experiment (Study 4) demonstrated that randomly assigning participants to enact identity distancing strategies over a week increased inauthenticity and disidentification compared to an identity affirming strategy. Together, these studies provide a multiple-identity examination of distancing strategies across diverse threatened identities, people, and situations, revealing psychological consequences of managing identities in the face of myriad everyday situations.

Title: Registered report stage I: Defending or defying democracy? Investigating the relationship between conspiracy beliefs and support for democratic principles [registered report - stage I]
Authors: Tisa Bertlich, Felicitas Flade, Roland Imhoff

Title: More is more, or is there more to it? Frequency moderations in evaluative conditioning depend on variation in the unconditioned stimuli
Authors: Mandy Hütter, Kathrin Reichmann, Dana Höffler, Marco Denin
Abstract: Evaluative conditioning (EC) is an experimental paradigm that models the acquisition of attitudes based on co-occurrences between conditioned stimuli (CSs) and unconditioned stimuli (USs). It has been noted that EC effects can be mediated by different forms of representations. Whereas stimulus-stimulus (S S) representations bring about an evaluative response via the CS's link to the specific US that it co-occurred with at learning, stimulus-valence (S V) representations entail a direct link between the CS and the valence category the US belongs to. The prevalence of these representations depends on US variability: S S representations are facilitated by procedures that repeat the same US at each presentation of the CS, S V representations are facilitated when a new US occurs at each pairing instance. The present research investigates whether EC effects develop differently depending on the variability of USs. Specifically, S S representations should emerge rapidly, whereas the abstraction underlying S V representations should benefit from repeated pairing instances. Across four experiments, we observed robust, largely valence-symmetric frequency moderations when a new US was shown at each pairing instance. In contrast, frequency moderations were generally absent when the same US was repeated, except in a procedure that intermixed same-US and different-USs pairings. These findings indicate that frequency and variability jointly shape EC effects and that such effects are mediated by the active construal of CS–US relations. This framework integrates previously inconsistent findings and underscores the theoretical importance of ecological variables and representational format for evaluative learning outcomes.

Title: Is a random human peer better than a highly supportive chatbot in reducing loneliness over time?
Authors: Ruo-Ning Li, Dunigan Folk, Abhay Singh, Lyle Ungar, Elizabeth Dunn
Abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly embedded in social life, offering accessible companionship. While brief interactions have been shown to provide immediate benefits, it is unclear whether repeated, daily engagement with chatbots reduces loneliness. In this pre-registered study, we tested the effectiveness of a chatbot versus a human peer in reducing loneliness among 296 students in their first semester of university. For two weeks, participants either interacted with a chatbot or a human peer, or simply wrote a brief journal entry (control condition). Although our chatbot “Sam” was designed to offer consistent support rooted in principles from relationship science, interacting with this chatbot did not yield the same psychological benefits as interacting with a randomly selected first-year university student. The present study provides initial evidence that texting daily with a random human peer may be more effective in alleviating loneliness than texting with a highly supportive chatbot.

Title: The effect of frameswitching on perceptions of decisiveness, creativity, and job fit
Authors: Sabrina Piccolo, Analía Albuja
Abstract: Multicultural people often adapt their behavior to the cultural contexts they are in (i.e., frameswitch). Although this behavior is common, it may have negative consequences for how others perceive Multicultural people's decisiveness and creativity. In three preregistered studies, participants read vignettes describing a Multicultural (White American and Chinese) target as frameswitching, not frameswitching, or without information about the target's behavior. Across all studies, participants viewed the target who frameswitched as less decisive than the no-frameswitching target. However, perceptions of the target's creativity were variable across operationalizations, with greater perceptions of willingness to transgress social norms but lower perceptions of general creativity and willingness to explore and no differences on external creativity or willingness to take on challenges. In Study 3, participants also rated how fit they perceived the target to be for four jobs that were rated as highly decisive and creative: carpenter, engineer, architect, and business owner. Participants perceived the target who frameswitched as less decisive than the target who did not frameswitch, which was associated with lower perceived fit for the jobs. These results suggest that people's evaluations of Multicultural people are shaped by how Multicultural people engage with their identities via frameswitching.

Title: Two wrongs is what makes it more right: How retaliatory incivility receives social leniency
Authors: Merrick R. Osborne, Suhaib Abdurahman, Ali Omrani, Jackson P. Trager, Morteza Dehghani
Abstract: Incivility is largely denounced; yet our focus on its ills has inhibited our ability to determine how incivility is evaluated depending on when it occurs. We propose that retaliatory incivility – i.e., incivility in response to someone else's incivility — is seen as less morally condemnable than instigatory incivility, and consequently leads the retaliator to receive more social leniency than the instigator. We experimentally confirm our hypotheses in a sample of Reddit users, as well as four samples of participants from different contexts of group incivility: hockey fans, baseball fans, employees, workplace teams. Together, our findings illustrate that evaluations of incivility in response to another's incivility (and directed at the instigator) are granted more social leniency than the instigator's incivility. Thus, as incivility rises internationally, our findings have far-reaching theoretical and practical implications.

Title: Gossip or confrontation? Sanctioning environmental norm violations and the reputation of punishers
Authors: Xiyan Song, Catherine Molho, Paul A.M. Van Lange
Abstract: Prior research has shown that peer punishment can promote norm adherence, but people's perceptions of whether and how environmentally harmful behaviors should be sanctioned remain underexplored. Shedding light on this question is important because normative consensus regarding environmental behaviors varies considerably, from strong and widely shared norms to weak or absent norms. Study 1 documents this normative variation by mapping norm perceptions across 18 environmentally friendly and harmful behaviors. Studies 2 and 3 examine the perceived appropriateness of different informal sanctions (i.e., gossip, exclusion, and confrontation) against environmentally harmful behaviors seen as norm violations. Further, we test how these sanctions affect punishers' reputation across several dimensions (i.e., warmth, morality, competence, and aggressiveness), as well as third parties' decisions to trust punishers. Results conceptually replicate previous work in the environmental domain by showing that more severe environmental norm violations led to higher perceived appropriateness of informal sanctions. Extending previous work, we also found that (1) gossip was perceived as the most appropriate informal sanction for moderate violations, while confrontation was perceived as most appropriate for severe violations, and that (2) punishers who confronted environmental norm breakers received a more favorable reputation and greater trust compared to those who responded with gossip or exclusion. This research suggests that informal sanctions are appropriate methods for addressing environmental norm violations, and their reputational consequences depend on the type of sanction used.

Title: Approach-avoidance action tendencies: A replicable approach/avoidance compatibility effect can be found when valence is task irrelevant
Authors: Yoann Julliard, Cédric Batailler, François Ric, Marine Rougier, Maude Tagand, Mae Braud, Dominique Muller
Abstract: Attitude objects (e.g., social groups) are assumed to elicit behavioral responses without thoughtful processing of their valence. Despite a theoretical consensus on this assumption, empirical evidence is mixed. To address this question, we provide evidence that approach-avoidance action tendencies are triggered by attitude objects when participants do not need to process objects' valence to perform the task. We did so with a version of the Visual Approach-Avoidance by the Self Task (VAAST, Rougier et al., 2018 ) in which participants were primed with a positive or negative word and then had to approach/avoid a neutral target. Across seven experiments we consistently found approach-avoidance compatibility effects (i.e., faster response times to approach a neutral target preceded by a positive [vs. negative] prime and to avoid a neutral target preceded by a negative [vs. positive] prime), even when introducing challenging manipulations. These effects yielded evidential p -values, they were robust across data-analytic decisions, and experiments were highly powered. This work corroborates theories predicting action triggering without thoughtful processing and could be the basis for studying action tendencies associated with various social stimuli (e.g., ingroup and outgroup individuals).

Title: Does ignorance love company? The social dynamics of information avoidance
Authors: Katharina Reher, Martin Götz, Filippo Toscano, Jörg Gross
Abstract: Individuals often avoid information about the social consequences of their actions when these conflict with their self-interest, thereby undermining prosocial behavior. Previous research has shown that individual factors affect who avoids information and under what circumstances. However, people often observe others' actions, update their perceptions of norms accordingly, and may inform each other about the negative consequences of their behavior. Here, we investigated how social dynamics influence information avoidance beyond personal preferences across four studies ( N = 760). Our findings reveal that social norms surrounding information avoidance changed based on the prevalence of the behavior. In an interactive experiment, people also mimicked others' actions, although this did not lead to an overall change in information avoidance and prosocial behavior. Interestingly, social influence was type-dependent. Selfish individuals were more prone to social influence, whereas prosocial individuals remained more consistent with their principles. In a second study, the ability to inform others about the negative consequences of their actions increased awareness and prosocial choices. However, the possibility of information sharing also diminished active information seeking. While primarily a minority of prosocial ‘information spreaders’ shared information, other individuals were less inclined to actively inform themselves. Overall, our results suggest that social influence plays a nuanced role in strategic information avoidance. Personal preferences interact with who ‘follows the crowd’ and shares information, or shifts the burden of seeking it. These findings underscore the importance of considering social dynamics alongside individual factors when studying how people avoid the inconvenient truths behind their decisions.

Title: Not all stimuli are conditioned equal – Larger evaluative conditioning effects for fluent stimuli
Authors: Claudine Pulm, Anne Gast
Abstract: Processing fluency, the subjective ease of ongoing mental operations, is known to influence evaluative outcomes. We tested how the ease with which the conditioned stimuli (CSs) in an evaluative conditioning (EC) experiment are processed influences how positively and negatively conditioned stimuli are evaluated. Across three experiments, we found evidence for amplifying fluency effects: fluent stimuli led to more extreme stimulus evaluations and thus stronger EC effects. In addition to the amplifying fluency effect, we also tested for hedonic effects of fluency – the overall more positive evaluation of fluently compared to disfluently processed stimuli. When fluency was manipulated as the pronounceability of different surnames, we indeed found more positive evaluations of fluently processed CSs. For a color contrast manipulation, fluent CSs were not evaluated more positively than disfluent ones. We outline implications both for understanding processing fluency and for EC.

Title: Using intersectional implicit association measures does not consistently improve the predictive validity of the implicit association test
Authors: Jeffrey To, Jordan Axt
Abstract: Historically, studies of implicit associations have mostly measured one identity at a time, such as investigating associations based on race or gender. Here, we explore whether intersectional implicit associations (e.g., attitudes toward Black men) predict relevant behavior better than implicit associations based on a single social identity (e.g., attitudes toward Black people). Across four studies (total N > 8000) using multiple measures of implicit attitudes, we find that these intersectional implicit associations were never better predictors of intergroup behavior than associations based on a single identity. Our findings challenge the assumption that greater correspondence between attitude and behavioral target enhances predictive validity, suggesting that, in time-pressured judgment contexts, perceivers may default to single-identity representations even for intersectional targets. This work highlights boundary conditions under which intersectional implicit measures are likely to add value.

Title: When rightness is wrong: Chronic prevention orientation predicts cardiovascular threat responses under regulatory fit
Authors: Deborah E. Ward, Mark D. Seery, Thomas L. Saltsman, Cheryl L. Kondrak
Abstract: Grounded in regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997) and the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge/Threat (BPSC/T; e.g., Blascovich, 2008), the present research tests the impact of chronic and situational regulatory orientations on cardiovascular responses during active goal pursuit. We propose two hypotheses: the “Non-Fit Threat Hypothesis,” which predicts that prevention-dominant individuals in promotion- (vs. prevention-) framed situations will evidence greater cardiovascular threat; and the “Prevention Threat Hypothesis,” which predicts that prevention-dominant individuals in prevention- (vs. promotion-) framed situations will evidence greater cardiovascular threat. Across two studies (N = 265), participants' cardiovascular responses were assessed during motivated performance situations (giving a speech, solving math problems). Findings were consistent with the Prevention Threat Hypothesis, such that prevention-dominant individuals exhibited greater cardiovascular threat during prevention-framed situations. This outcome contrasts with previous research emphasizing the benefits of regulatory fit for motivation and performance outcomes, but aligns with evidence suggesting that prevention-dominance amplifies sensitivity to situational demands during active goal pursuit. Results highlight the role of regulatory focus in shaping real-time psychological states. Importantly, future research should extend the present and previous findings using different conceptualizations of fit versus non-fit situations.

Title: When society feels broken: How perceptions of anomie shape donation tendencies across cultures
Authors: Fei Gao, Lan Xia
Abstract: Across five studies, this research examines how perceived anomie, defined as individuals' perception of societal breakdown, influences donation tendencies and identifies the underlying psychological mechanisms and cultural conditions shaping this relationship. We distinguish between two dimensions of anomie: leadership anomie (perceived failure of government leadership) and moral anomie (perceived erosion of shared moral norms). Studies 1a and 1b (correlational, conducted in the U.S. (individualistic culture) and China (collectivistic culture) show that higher perceived leadership anomie is consistently associated with lower donation tendencies through reduced perceived personal responsibility and efficacy of contributions in both cultural contexts. In contrast, higher perceived moral anomie was associated with lower donation tendencies in China, and this association was mediated by reduced personal responsibility and efficacy; no such association was observed in the U.S. Studies 2 and 3 employed experiments to establish causality. Studies 2a and 2b manipulated perceived leadership anomie in China and the U.S., respectively, and showed that heightened perceptions reduced donation tendencies through diminished responsibility and efficacy. Study 3 manipulated perceived moral anomie and replicated the culturally contingent effect: donation tendencies declined in China but not in the U.S. Study 3 further demonstrated that this reduction in China was mediated by lower perceived personal responsibility and efficacy of contributions. This research contributes to the literature on anomie, prosociality, and moral psychology by demonstrating how perceived leadership and moral breakdowns shape helping behavior and by identifying culturally contingent mechanisms through which these effects occur.

Title: Unequal participation: How low socioeconomic status hinders political engagement
Authors: Rodrigo Furst, Yan Vieites, Bernardo Andretti
Abstract: Political participation is a key mechanism through which individuals express their preferences in democratic systems. Thus, unequal participation may allow some groups to exert disproportionate influence on political outcomes. This research examines the existence of socioeconomic status (SES) differences in political engagement and sheds light on the psychological mechanisms driving these disparities across seven studies. Using nationwide surveys from 47 countries ( N = 70,417), Study 1 reveals an SES gap in political engagement across various domains (e.g., voting, boycotting) and shows that this gap is partly due to lower political efficacy—one's perceived ability to influence political affairs—among low-SES individuals. Study 2 ( N = 545) replicates these findings in a representative sample of the Brazilian population, using a behavioral proxy for political participation. Studies 3a-c ( N 3a = 301; N 3b = 302; N 3c = 301) experimentally manipulate SES among U.S. participants and show that effectively inducing lower-SES perceptions reduces political engagement. Studies 4a-b ( N 4a = 301; N 4b = 328) test an intervention in a lab-in-the-field experiment with extremely deprived residents of Rio de Janeiro's slums, showing that enhancing political efficacy increases participation among low-SES individuals both in the run-up to and in the aftermath of a national election. Together, these studies demonstrate that while SES is consistently linked to political participation, addressing psychological barriers and fostering political efficacy can help close the participation gap. In addition, this work contributes to broader methodological debates surrounding the measurement and experimental manipulation of socioeconomic conditions in psychological research.

Title: Beyond confronting: Cultivating inclusion through proactive Allyship
Authors: Lucy De Souza, Toni Schmader
Abstract: Historically marginalized group members encounter barriers to belonging and inclusion, even when instances of interpersonal bias are rare. While allyship (ongoing behaviors in support of those with less societal status; De Souza & Schmader, 2025) includes confronting bias when one sees it, we sought to establish the unique benefits of proactive allyship for those who have gained access to certain domains but remain underrepresented (Flam, 1991; Walton et al., 2015). Across five studies, we apply a novel framework ( The Typology of Allyship Action ; De Souza & Schmader, 2025) to empirically differentiate and compare inclusion-related benefits unique to proactive action. Study 1 uses newly developed scenario-based materials to validate theoretical distinctions between proactive and reactive action, i.e., proactive action's greater flexibility in time, focus on disadvantaged group members, and aim of fostering positive outcomes. Applying these scenarios, Studies 2–3 used experimental methods to assess perceptions of proactive action's (compared to reactive action's and inaction's) impact on both gender and race-based inclusion. Moving beyond hypothetical scenarios, Study 4 tested how proactive (compared to reactive) action predicts actual workplace experiences amongst women in STEM. Across studies, preregistered hypotheses were supported: proactive allyship was consistently perceived and experienced as particularly beneficial in promoting workplace inclusion, feelings of fit, and success for disadvantaged group members. These findings broaden theoretical conceptions and practical applications of allyship, demonstrating the importance of allyship beyond confrontation.

Title: Playing it safe: Negotiators avoid uncertainty and reach safer, but less integrative agreements
Authors: Marco Schauer, Johann M. Majer, Caroline Heydenbluth, Roman Trötschel
Abstract: Social-interactive conflict management processes inherently involve uncertainties about the exact outcomes that agreements may yield. However, two literature reviews show that irrespective of the inherent uncertainty of most real-world social decision-making contexts, experimental negotiation studies have traditionally relied on certain outcome scenarios so that it remains unknown whether and how outcome uncertainty affects interactive logrolling and therefore agreement quality. In contrast, we propose and test two competing hypotheses on how outcome uncertainty may affect social-interactive joint decision-making. On the one hand, the Value-Insight Hypothesis suggests that focusing on the value component of uncertain outcomes highlights priority differences between conflict parties, thereby facilitating parties' interactive exploration of integrative priority-based trade-offs. On the other hand, the Uncertainty- Avoidance Hypothesis argues that focusing on the risk component of uncertain outcomes leads to mutual uncertainty-avoidant trade-offs that hinder parties to explore integrative priority-based trade-offs. We introduce novel social decision-making paradigms to systematically test these competing hypotheses in a causal chain design. Specifically, across three pre-registered ( N = 502) interactive negotiation studies, we find that in line with the Uncertainty-Avoidance Hypothesis parties' sensitivity to explore priority-differences is reduced under uncertainty. Across different operationalizations of outcome uncertainty parties reach less integrative agreements for uncertain compared to certain outcomes. In fact, parties reached more compromising agreements under uncertainty irrespective of varying levels and ranges of risks (Study 2). Beyond uncertainty-avoidance, parties reached lower-quality agreements under uncertainty even in contexts in which no mutual trade-offs allowed them to reduce or avoid uncertainty (Study 3).

Title: Tracking connections, not content: How working memory shapes content and social learning in online networks
Authors: Esther Kang, Arun Lakshmanan
Abstract: How do individuals navigate and prioritize social information in online networks? While social networks provide continuous streams of content, they also constitute complex webs of social connections. Across five studies, we show that individuals with higher working memory capacity do not necessarily learn more from the content itself. Instead, they strategically allocate attention toward mapping social relationships, such as tracking who is connected to whom, effectively treating the network as an external social memory system. This attentional reallocation leads to reduced engagement with content but enhanced encoding of relational structures. These findings highlight a counterintuitive role of working memory in digital social cognition: cognitive resources are deployed to optimize learning about social connections rather than content, reflecting adaptive strategies for managing relational information. Theoretically, this work advances understanding of how attention and memory support social learning in digital environments.

Title: Why do people dislike gender role violators? A test of three models
Authors: Alan J. Lambert, Fade R. Eadeh, Svyatoslav Prokhorets, Giselle Gisser, Keralyn Siebrass
Abstract: People often react negatively towards individuals whose attributes clash with traditional gender roles (e.g., feminine men, masculine women). However, some important ambiguities remain about the underlying processes driving these effects. This gap is particularly important with respect to the role of perceived sexual orientation (i.e., whether the target is seen as non-heterosexual or straight). In this article, we examine whether gender role violations directly cause backlash (Hypothesis 1), influence backlash through perceived non-heterosexuality for all perceivers (indirect hypothesis, Hypothesis 2), or if these indirect effects depend on levels of right-wing authoritarianism (moderation hypothesis, Hypothesis 3). Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 2351) we found strongest support for Hypothesis 3. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of our findings concerning understanding—and potentially reducing—negative reactions towards others whose attributes deviate from traditional expectations.

Title: Minority report: How minorities' awareness of power asymmetry drives strategic preparation in opinion debates
Authors: Alain Quiamzade, Fanny Lalot, Dominic Abrams
Abstract: Minority influence research has focused on the processes through which minority influence can occur (i.e., deep processing) but neglected to test whether minorities actually solicit these processes (i.e., prepare stronger messages). The present research addresses this fundamental gap. We propose that people (i) intuitively grasp the need for the minority to be more prepared than a majority, and (ii) act accordingly. A pilot and five studies ( N = 1584) tested these hypotheses using a debate paradigm. Studies 1–4 demonstrated that participants are generally aware of the asymmetry between majorities and minorities (defined by their representation in the general population rather than numbers involved in the interaction; Study 2). This awareness applied both when participants judged the behavior of others (Studies 1–3) and when personally involved in a debate situation, either imagined (Study 3) or anticipated as real (Study 4). The asymmetrical need to prepare is also manifested in preparatory behavior. Participants reported having prepared more when they expected to defend the minority position (Study 4) and objectively prepared more in a controlled laboratory setting (Study 5). Further, preparatory behavior was partially mediated by awareness of the greater need to prepare (Study 4). We discuss implications for minority influence, persuasion, and collective action research.

Title: Decision strategy and perceived humanness: The roles of decision context and decision outcome
Authors: Hong Zhang, Huan Zhu, Jingyan Wang, Yima Jin
Abstract: Four studies (three pre-registered), varying in design and measures, investigated the effect of decision strategy (i.e., intuitive vs. deliberative) on humanness perceptions. Main findings include 1) individuals attributed higher humanness to deliberative than intuitive decision-makers, except for the experience dimension, 2) a congruence effect emerged such that the discrepancy in humanness perceptions of deliberative versus intuitive decision makers was smaller in social than non-social domains, 3) perceived outcome partially mediated the interaction between decision strategy and decision context on humanness perceptions, and 4) the association between decision strategy and humanness perceptions was moderated by gender and individual differences in lay rationalism. Implications for future studies on decision process and humanness perceptions are discussed.

Title: The effects of anonymity in volunteer's dilemmas
Authors: Yukari Jessica Tham, Yohsuke Ohtsubo, Kaori Karasawa
Abstract: Groups often face volunteer's dilemmas—situations in which a single member's contribution is both necessary and sufficient to benefit all, such that additional contributions create inefficiency. In Experiments 1 and 2 (total N = 332), we examined whether removing anonymity promotes volunteering in incentivized two-person volunteer's dilemma games. Results showed that removing anonymity increased volunteering rates when players' volunteering costs were equal or only moderately different within a dyad. However, when the cost difference was large, the volunteering rates of high-cost players, whose contributions were especially likely to create inefficiency, remained low even when anonymity was removed. Experiment 3 ( N = 346) demonstrated that abstaining from volunteering was unlikely to damage these high-cost players' reputations. These findings identify a boundary condition of the effects of removing anonymity: its ability to promote cooperative behavior is constrained by a heightened risk of inefficiency.

Title: Learning to distrust: One trust experience changes the expected value of trust
Authors: Annabelle R. Roberts, Emma E. Levine, Jane L. Risen
Abstract: Do people learn from a single trust interaction? Using internal meta-analyses with twenty-one studies (N = 11,899), we find that feedback about the trustworthiness of one interaction partner influences the decision to trust a new person in a subsequent interaction. People are more likely to trust a new individual after positive feedback about an initial partner and less likely to trust a new individual after negative feedback about an initial partner. A single piece of feedback influences the expected value of trust by changing both the perceived probability that an individual in the relevant population is trustworthy as well as the expected emotional consequences (i.e., utility) of trust. Both mechanisms may help explain why people learn from a single trust interaction. We further find that trust behavior is most affected by exploitation: People are particularly unlikely to trust a new person when they previously trusted an untrustworthy person. These findings suggest that people rely on past experiences to guide trust decisions with new individuals, leading people to learn to distrust.

Title: Emotional cues to group hierarchy: Inferences about dominance- versus prestige-based hierarchies from members' emotional expressions
Authors: Marc W. Heerdink, Svenja A. Wolf, Jens Lange, Florian Wanders, Xia Fang, Eftychia Stamkou, Gerben A. van Kleef
Abstract: Dominance and prestige are both strategies to attain rank. They are differentially effective depending on whether the group's hierarchy is based primarily on dominance or prestige. Insight into the nature of the group's hierarchy is therefore essential for upward mobility. But how do people obtain such insight? In five studies (two pre-registered; combined N = 2470), we investigated whether people use group members' emotional expressions to draw inferences about the degree to which a group's hierarchy is dominance- or prestige-based. We distinguished among three theoretical accounts: (1) a valence account, which posits that negative emotions convey that hierarchies are more dominance- and less prestige-based than positive emotions; (2) a social engagement account, which holds that socially engaging emotions convey that hierarchies are more prestige- and less dominance-based than socially disengaging emotions; and (3) a discrete-emotions account, which suggests that only a few specific emotions convey information about the predominant hierarchy type. We tested these predictions from the perspective of group members and outside observers, reporting experimental evidence on the effects of five emotional expressions (happy, proud, neutral, sad, angry). Our findings support a combined valence and social engagement account: Expressions of positive emotions signal a more prestige- and less dominance-based hierarchy than negative emotions, and among emotions of similar valence, expressions of socially engaging emotions signal a more prestige- and less dominance-based hierarchy than disengaging emotions. Extending the work on affective processes in hierarchy, we conclude that emotional expressions provide important cues about how rank is typically attained in groups.

Title: Holiday greeting inclusivity in organizations: The more the merrier
Authors: Erica L. Granz Nack, Kimberly Rios
Abstract: As America becomes more religiously diverse, it is critical to investigate how to create holiday messaging that both dominant and non-dominant religious groups perceive as inclusive. We conducted four experiments to investigate the effect of different levels of specificity for winter and spring holiday greetings on participant perceptions of belonging and diversity importance at ostensibly real organizations. The message was either for a Christian holiday (e.g., “Merry Christmas”), a current general inclusive greeting (e.g., “Happy Holidays”), or a more specific inclusive greeting with three cultural holidays mentioned (e.g., “Happy Hanukkah, Merry Christmas, Joyous Kwanzaa”). Overall, the three-holiday message elicited the highest feelings of belonging and was perceived as reflecting the most openness to diversity. A single-paper meta-analysis suggested this is especially true among non-Christian participants. Implications for how to approach diverse holiday messages in organizational settings are discussed.

Title: The spread of fear: Perceptual deindividuation drives racial bias in threat generalization
Authors: Arshiya Aggarwal, Julia R. Hopkins, Dana E. Diaz, Kalina J. Michalska, Nicholas P. Camp, Brent L. Hughes
Abstract: Fear often generalizes beyond its original source, yet little is known about how race shapes its consequences for threat misidentification. In a fear conditioning paradigm, 284 racially diverse participants learned to associate an aversive sound with one Black and one White face. We then assessed participants' physiological responses and behavioral threat identification judgments to novel faces varying in similarity to the original target; behavioral analyses included 255 participants and physiological (SCR) analyses included 188 participants after standard exclusions for task withdrawal and SCR non-responsiveness. Although physiological responses tracked physical similarity regardless of race, behavioral responses revealed a racial asymmetry in generalization: participants were more likely to identify novel Black faces as the original source of threat. Sigmoid modeling showed that participants applied a lower perceptual threshold when identifying Black faces as the source of threat. These asymmetries were most pronounced among individuals high in general threat sensitivity, who relied less on perceptual similarity when evaluating Black faces, resulting in more frequent threat misidentification. These findings may inform our understanding of real-world disparities by highlighting how racial categorization shapes the misidentification of threat, and how learned threat can spread across group members.

Title: Trust under watch: Relational models and the context-dependent nature of monitoring
Authors: Anna O. Kuzminska, Maryam Khan, Pelin Kesebir, Tomasz Zaleskiewicz, Agata Gasiorowska
Abstract: Trust and control are often portrayed as opposing forces in a hydraulic relationship. Across six preregistered experiments (total N = 4086) conducted in Australia, South Africa, the UK, and the US, we demonstrate that this relationship is context-dependent rather than universal. We examined how verification monitoring—a subtle form of control—affects trust in communal sharing (CS) versus market pricing (MP) relationships. Participants found monitoring more acceptable in MP than CS relationships (Experiment 1), and its introduction shifted perceptions of CS relationships toward a more market-like orientation (Experiments S1-S2). From the trustee's perspective, monitoring reduced trust in both relational contexts; from the trustor's view, it only undermined trust in CS relationships (Experiment 2). These patterns generalized across cultures, held across different trust levels (Experiment 3), and extended to behavioral choices (Experiment 4). Our findings challenge the universality of the hydraulic model, showing that while control mechanisms undermine trust in communal contexts where they violate norms of unconditional support, their effects in market contexts depend on whose perspective is considered—trustors or trustees.

Title: Beyond morality primacy: Inference of competence takes the lead in spontaneous impressions
Authors: Irmak Olcaysoy Okten, Xi Shen, Ayanna Brewton
Abstract: Past research has shown that morality plays a stronger role than competence in driving our social impressions. It is not clear, however, whether morality plays a primary role in spontaneous impressions that are formed effortlessly and without an explicit intention to form an impression. Four studies (N total = 746) tested spontaneous morality and competence inferences from behavioral descriptions with a false recognition paradigm. This paradigm not only allowed us to test the spontaneity in inferring morality versus competence traits from behaviors but also enabled us to tease apart the processes of trait accessibility and binding in memory. Across Experiments 1–3, perceivers were more likely to make spontaneous trait inferences (STIs) from competence (vs. morality) information by binding inferred traits to the relevant actors, indicating competence primacy. Experiment 4 compared spontaneous and intentional inferences and showed that although morality traits were more readily accessible in memory than competence traits when impressions were formed intentionally, competence traits remained more likely to be bound to relevant actors. Together, these findings suggest that morality does not hold primacy in spontaneous impression formation.

Title: Interpersonal synchrony modulates explicit and implicit self-other blurring: Evidence from an IAT
Authors: Manisha Biswas, Marcel Brass
Abstract: The transformative effects of interpersonal synchrony on reshaping the relationship between the self and the group by fostering self-other blurring are well-documented. However, this account relies largely on self-reported measures, leaving aspects of the self inaccessible to explicit measures unexplored. We combined the Implicit Association Task (IAT) with conventional explicit evaluations of self-other blurring to examine whether experiences of synchronous movement also swiftly shape implicit measures indicative of self-other blurring. In three online experiments, participants experienced synchronous movement as opposed to no movement (Experiment 1), unpredictable movement (Experiment 2) or asynchronous movement (Experiment 3) with virtually presented agents. Our data indicate that synchronous movement led to higher levels of self-other overlap on the Inclusion of Other in Self (IOS) scale and on implicit self-concept evaluations on the Implicit Association Test (IAT). Participants demonstrated a preference for associating self-related words with images of the synchronous group and associating other-related words with images from the no-movement, unpredictable, and asynchronous movement groups. These findings demonstrate that interpersonal synchrony alters self-concept at both an explicit and implicit level, extending beyond conscious reports of affiliation. Our combined methodology offers a deeper insight into the impact of synchronous experiences on self-constructs and social relationships.

Title: Common = ineffective? A replication attempt of the normative dilution effect in the context of political apologies
Authors: Vlada Trofimchuk, Rebecca Littman
Abstract: The normative dilution effect suggests that perceiving a behavior as normative can undermine its effectiveness, particularly in contexts where its communicative value matters. Intergroup apologies offer a compelling test case for this effect, as conveying sincere motives is key to their effectiveness in promoting forgiveness. To date, only one quantitative study (Okimoto, et al., 2015) has tested this effect. We therefore aimed to replicate the normative dilution effect a decade after the original study in two experimental studies. Across two samples of Australian participants ( N total = 1075), we found no evidence supporting the normative dilution effect.
